title: Intercultural Competence
audience: All staff, including supervisors and managers
outcomes: Explain how cultural meaning influences an ordinary exchange without predicting a person from identity.
Separate what was observed from what was assumed and check another person’s meaning.
Choose a useful adjustment to a service conversation or workplace interaction.
Recognize when one familiar communication style has become the standard for everyone.
summary: Build your understanding of cultural perspectives and see how everyday choices shape DSD services and workplace opportunity for the people you serve and the colleagues you work with.
body:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Intercultural Competence

Understanding cultural perspectives and how everyday choices shape DSD services and workplace opportunity.

Self-directed Foundation learning for all staff

Your learning

Consider each practice situation privately. You do not need to disclose personal, employee, or case information.

Choose a response, read its explanation, and reconsider what you know and what remains uncertain.

Look beyond intent: whose participation could the action change, especially if it becomes routine?

Different ways of seeing

A service discussion accepts comments only during the meeting. Someone needs more time or another way to contribute.

Their knowledge may be missed. Repeating that format can narrow whose experience shapes services.

Before reading on, choose one change and explain what you would need to check with participants.

Belonging and group identity

Unwritten expectations can leave a newcomer unsure how to contribute. Their silence may then be mistaken for lack of interest.

If that judgment shapes later assignments, an onboarding gap can become an opportunity gap.

Make expectations clear and ask what would help. What evidence would change your first interpretation?

Practice: a service explanation

A person sets a translated renewal notice aside. Their family offers to answer every question. What would best support a respectful discussion?

A. Rely on the family’s answers because the notice was translated.

B. Ask the person how they prefer to review the steps and whom they want involved.

C. Record that the person is uninterested in the renewal.

In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Intention and impact

A staff member answers for a person to be helpful. The person loses the chance to explain their priorities.

If this becomes routine, plans may reflect other people’s assumptions rather than the person’s wishes.

Return the conversation to the person and ask about chosen support. What would you change next time?

Understanding another perspective

A person’s meaning of independence may include close family relationships. Staff may assume it means doing everything alone.

That assumption can narrow the support options discussed and become embedded in planning routines.

Ask what the person wants and who they want involved. A brief prepares questions; the person explains their meaning.

The Golden Rule

The Golden Rule encourages the care and respect we would want to receive.

Using only our preferred approach may still make information or feedback harder for another person to use.

Ask what works for them. Which of your own preferences could become an unnecessary requirement?

The Platinum Rule

The Platinum Rule asks us to learn how another person wishes to be treated.

Adjust an explanation, meeting format, or feedback approach when appropriate; explain any limits clearly.

Check whether the change helped. A repeated adjustment may reveal a default that needs review.

Intercultural competence

Intercultural competence connects understanding cultural meaning with an appropriate response.

Ask whose expectations shape a service or workplace routine and how that routine affects participation.

Try an adjustment supported by what you learn. What would show that it helped rather than merely changed the interaction? This course does not assess anyone’s intercultural development.

Practice: onboarding and belonging

A new employee contributes in writing but rarely speaks during meetings. The team describes them as disengaged. What would deepen its understanding?

A. Ask about participation preferences and examine written contributions alongside other relevant evidence.

B. Explain the behavior by assigning the employee a cultural identity.

C. Use the learning discussion to identify the employee’s IDI orientation.

In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Intercultural Development Continuum

The continuum describes Denial, Polarization, Minimization, Acceptance, and Adaptation as orientations toward cultural difference.

Use it to examine practice approaches and what they may overlook, not to label people.

A course answer or helpful action cannot establish anyone’s IDI result.

Denial

Denial involves limited attention to cultural difference or difficulty recognizing its relevance.

An unfamiliar perspective may never enter a service or onboarding discussion. Repeated omissions can shape what the system notices.

Whose experience could widen the question? Identify a way to learn without labeling anyone.

Polarization

Polarization frames difference through “us and them.” Defense favors one’s own group; Reversal devalues it in favor of another.

Dismissing knowledge by group can silence concerns and narrow the evidence used in decisions.

What is the specific concern, and what could each perspective help explain?

Minimization

Minimization emphasizes common needs while overlooking differences that affect participation.

The same notice or onboarding package may be unusable for some people. Reusing it can preserve the access gap.

What difference matters to this shared goal, and how could the requirement become usable?

Acceptance

Acceptance recognizes meaningful cultural differences alongside common ground.

Explore what independence, support, or professional growth means to the person before offering options.

Understanding improves the decision’s basis; leaving the routine unchanged may still leave a barrier. What response deserves consideration?

Practice: community participation

A familiar community partner comments on a proposed service change. The team treats that response as the community’s view. What should it consider next?

A. Proceed because a community representative has responded.

B. Use a culture brief to decide what everyone in the community would prefer.

C. Explore whose perspectives are missing and how those affected can shape the discussion.

In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Adaptation

Adaptation involves considering another cultural perspective and adjusting behavior appropriately.

Change an explanation, meeting approach, or feedback conversation in response to what you learn.

Ask what improved and what remains difficult. If the barrier recurs, consider whether the routine also needs attention.

Practice: a translated notice

A person sets a translated renewal notice aside and says they have no questions.

Assuming understanding may leave next steps unclear; repeated assumptions can make the notice an access barrier.

Choose an open question about format or next steps. What could the answer establish that the action alone cannot?

Practice: a loud conversation

A caller speaks loudly about a service delay. Staff begin to interpret the volume as hostility.

An unsupported label could change the response and travel into later records or decisions.

Consider what was said and the communication conditions. How would you describe the exchange without guessing intent?

Practice: an earlier complaint

A person previously raised a discrimination concern. Staff expect the next conversation to be difficult.

That expectation may narrow listening and become a label that follows the person through later contacts.

How could you acknowledge the concern while hearing the current question on its own evidence?

Practice: an offer of support

A family declines an option and calls it “welfare.” Their meaning and the person’s own wishes remain unknown.

Pressure to accept may weaken trust; recording a group assumption can affect later offers.

How could you explore concerns, explain choices, and respect the person’s decision without predicting beliefs from identity?

Continuing the learning

Choose one service or workplace routine and trace how it could affect voice, access, or opportunity.

Prepare with a brief, listen to the people affected, and consider a response within your responsibility.

Name what you would check afterward. One DSD connects this learning with accessibility, cultural humility, community engagement, and equity review.

title: Cultural Humility in Everyday Public Service
audience: All staff, including supervisors and managers
outcomes: Cultural humility means continuing to pay attention to your own assumptions, your relationships and the influence you hold in public service. This course explains what that looks like day to day.
Receive a correction without expecting another person to teach or reassure you.
Use information about a community as preparation rather than as a personal profile.
Recognize how a routine can preserve the staff member’s interpretation after the person has challenged it.
summary: Cultural humility means continuing to pay attention to your own assumptions, your relationships and the influence you hold in public service. This course explains what that looks like day to day.
body:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Cultural Humility in Everyday Public Service
Learning from another person’s meaning while examining how our assumptions and influence shape services and workplace opportunity.
Foundation self-directed learning

When help carries an assumption
An offer of help can be caring and still miss what another person wants.

A person declines help. Before deciding they are reluctant, consider two meanings the refusal could have.

Which question would let their answer change your first interpretation?

What cultural humility involves
Cultural humility means continuing self-examination, openness to another person’s account, and attention to unequal influence.

Knowledge informs the question; it does not answer for the individual.

You can reconsider an assumption while keeping necessary standards and responsibilities clear.

A planning conversation to reconsider
Staff invite family because they assume family involvement is always helpful. The person requests a private conversation.

Overriding that request could leave the person’s priorities unheard. Repeating the assumption may shape plans around others’ wishes.

Ask about chosen support and the arrangement the person wants.

Practice: chosen support
Staff invite family to planning. The person asks to speak privately. Staff say family involvement is usually helpful. Which response keeps the person’s wishes central?
A. Keep the invitation because the team knows what usually works.
B. Ask about the preferred arrangement and chosen support within the appropriate process.
C. Cancel planning until staff know the person’s cultural background.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Your knowledge is a starting point
Experience can help you anticipate useful questions. It can also make one explanation feel certain too soon.

Separate what the source describes from what this person has said.

Which detail could challenge the familiar explanation?

Meaning and preference are not identical
Two people may value family while wanting different support in a particular conversation.

Ask what participation means now, rather than treating a shared value as a fixed instruction.

Circumstances and preferences can change; keep room for a later correction.

Influence matters in an ordinary exchange
The person arranging an agenda, recording a concern, or assigning work can make their interpretation consequential.

Being invited to speak is different from being able to influence an open choice.

Explain what can change and which limits are real.

When someone corrects your account
A correction supplies information your first interpretation missed.

Acknowledge the specific change, revise what you can, and avoid asking the person to reassure you.

If the old account remains in a record or routine, a private change of mind may not repair its effects.

One way to demonstrate commitment?
A newcomer asks to send considered comments after a meeting. An experienced colleague says committed staff speak immediately.

That expectation may hide useful knowledge. If it shapes feedback, it can narrow later development opportunities.

Clarify the actual work need before treating a familiar style as the standard.

Practice: contribution during onboarding
A new employee offers written comments after a meeting. A colleague says committed staff speak immediately. What would clarify the expectation fairly?
A. Examine the actual work need, written contribution, and usable ways to respond.
B. Record limited commitment because the employee did not follow the usual style.
C. Assume their identity explains the preference and stop asking.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

An onboarding gap can travel forward
Unexplained expectations can make a newcomer’s contribution harder to recognize.

A judgment made early may later shape supervision, assignments, and advancement.

Check the work evidence and the introduction provided before deciding what the gap means.

Respectful support includes clear limits
Listening does not require agreeing with every request or promising an unavailable option.

Explain the actual constraint and distinguish it from a preferred way of working.

A feasible alternative may preserve the purpose while improving participation.

A brief prepares you to listen
Community briefs introduce history, institutions, and context; they do not predict an individual.

Use a brief to notice a question you might otherwise miss.

Hear current, varied perspectives without asking one person to represent everyone.

Partnership needs a genuine choice
A request for input should explain what people can influence and how their knowledge will be considered.

Listening without considering a relevant change may leave the same barrier in place.

Participation can be useful without assigning community members the staff’s work.

When a useful correction is dismissed
A participant says appointment instructions identify the building but not the entrance. Staff reply that the address is correct.

The fact is accurate, yet the route may remain unusable. Repeated dismissal favors insider knowledge.

What could the participant’s account help staff examine?

Practice: an instruction people can use
A participant says appointment instructions do not identify the entrance. Staff reply that the building address is correct. What would make their knowledge useful?
A. Keep the instructions because the official address is accurate.
B. Treat the account as proof that every person needs the same change.
C. Ask what was unclear, consider a usable revision, and explain what input can change.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

A checklist can support humility
A checklist can help make language, access, and participation questions visible.

Completing it cannot establish a person’s preferences or make an unresolved answer true.

Use the tool to support inquiry and revise the account when information changes.

Follow the interpretation downstream
An assumption can enter a note, shape the next conversation, and become a reason to offer fewer choices.

Ask where the account is reused and who can review it.

Correcting the immediate exchange may be a beginning; recurring effects need attention to the routine.

Ask what the response changed
A clearer explanation or revised invitation is a useful action.

Ask whether the people affected could use it and what remained difficult.

No new feedback does not prove the barrier disappeared; retain the unanswered question.

Rewrite an interpretation
Choose a practice example: “declined help,” “quiet in the meeting,” or “questioned the instruction.”

Write what was observed, one assumption to reconsider, and a question that could change it.

Then explain how leaving the assumption unchanged might affect a later choice.

Keep the learning open
Cultural humility connects self-examination, listening, influence, and a considered response.

You can value your experience while letting another account change your interpretation.

Continue with community briefs, person-centered learning, and equity review when they help clarify the question.

title: Cultural Identity, Assumptions, and the Meaning of Normal
audience: All staff, including supervisors and managers
outcomes: Culture is learned, varied and always changing, and that includes professional and workplace cultures. This course helps you see how those cultures shape assumptions about what counts as normal.
Notice how one’s own experience influences expectations about time, family, communication, and work.
Distinguish a carefully qualified group pattern from an unsupported conclusion about an individual.
Explain how an expectation becomes consequential when it is built into a public process.
summary: Culture is learned, varied and always changing, and that includes professional and workplace cultures. This course helps you see how those cultures shape assumptions about what counts as normal.
body:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Cultural Identity, Assumptions, and the Meaning of Normal
Explore how learned expectations become familiar standards, and how to keep them open to evidence and another person’s meaning.
Foundation self-directed learning

Where did normal come from?
A host offers everyone a shared meal as a welcome. Someone declines and asks to sit nearby instead.

Before deciding the person is unfriendly, consider what the invitation and refusal could mean.

Which part is observed, and which part comes from the host’s expectation?

Culture is learned, varied, and changing
Culture includes learned meanings and practices shaped by relationships, language, place, professions, and communities.

People have several affiliations, and their meaning can change across settings or time.

An identity does not establish every preference, ability, or belief.

When a form assumes the answer
A service form asks for “the household decision-maker.” The person says they make their own choices and want support for one topic.

Treating the household as one decision unit could hide the person’s agency.

What question would clarify the individual’s wishes without assuming authority for someone else?

Practice: a question about decision-making
A form asks for the household decision-maker. The person says they make their own choices and want support for one topic. What should staff clarify?
A. Which household member usually speaks, using the community brief as the answer.
B. The person’s wishes and chosen support for the decision at hand.
C. Whether the person can prove they belong to a culture that values independence.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

A value is not a universal instruction
You can value teamwork without requiring everyone to show it in the same way.

Distinguish the purpose from the familiar behavior used to express it.

What could meet the work need while allowing another effective approach?

Your perspective is part of the account
A route can seem clear to an experienced employee and confusing to a newcomer.

Neither account alone describes every condition.

Ask which information is available to each person and what could change your interpretation.

Professional culture also has defaults
Terms, meeting habits, and ideas about a strong contribution can become familiar within a profession.

A newcomer or community participant may encounter them as unexplained requirements.

Keep necessary expertise clear while making the route to participation understandable.

A flattering prediction can restrict someone
“Younger staff are naturally good with technology” sounds positive but does not establish skill or interest.

Automatic assignments can add unwanted work and limit others’ learning.

Ask about demonstrated ability, relevant interest, and the actual work requirement.

When familiarity becomes “fit”
A recruitment discussion praises a candidate for sharing the team’s hobbies and conversational style.

Those similarities may feel comfortable without showing readiness for the work.

What relevant criterion and evidence would make the comparison clearer?

Practice: familiarity in recruitment
A candidate is praised as a good fit because they share the team’s hobbies. Relevant work evidence is still incomplete. What would improve the comparison?
A. Clarify the work criterion and compare relevant evidence consistently.
B. Treat shared interests as proof that the candidate will perform well.
C. Reject the candidate because familiarity must mean unfair treatment.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Role and authority amplify an expectation
A preference carries more weight when expressed by someone who assigns work or reviews performance.

Employees may hear a casual suggestion as a condition for opportunity.

State the actual expectation and where another approach can meet it.

Small gates can connect across employment
Informal welcome, insider guidance, and familiar networks can affect access to early assignments.

Those assignments can become evidence of readiness for later advancement.

Trace the route before explaining the whole outcome as individual ability or commitment.

Group evidence has a proper scope
A group-level pattern can identify an equity question without predicting every individual.

Keep the population, question, time, and missing information visible.

Use the finding to examine a process; ask individuals about the needs relevant to their own situation.

A brief is context, not a person
Community briefs offer history and context that can widen the questions you ask.

They cannot establish the individual’s view, preference, or readiness.

Listen to varied current accounts and keep Native American and Tribal-specific matters within referral guidance.

Preserve the concern without a group label
Several participants say an appointment instruction is confusing. A draft calls the whole community unable to understand policy.

The draft changes an instruction concern into a claim about people.

What wording would retain the access question and its evidence limits?

Practice: a concern without a profile
Several participants find an appointment instruction confusing. A draft says the whole community cannot understand policy. Which revision respects the evidence?
A. Remove all community information and stop examining the notice.
B. Give everyone in the category mandatory extra explanation.
C. Describe the particular difficulty, its known scope, and the instruction question still open.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Let new evidence change the expectation
Calling every contrary example an exception protects a stereotype from examination.

Revise the claim to match the actual evidence rather than replace it with an opposite absolute.

Consider whether the old assumption still controls a record or decision.

Respect individuality and retain equity inquiry
An individual account does not establish a whole group’s experience.

A supported group pattern should not disappear because it cannot describe everyone.

Use each kind of knowledge for the question it can help answer.

Rewrite one familiar expectation
Choose a practice statement: “good fit,” “naturally skilled,” or “not interested.”

Replace it with the relevant task, observed evidence, and a question still open.

Explain how the original expectation could affect service choice or development if repeated.

Understanding can change before a routine does
Recognizing an assumption is a meaningful learning gain.

If the assumption shaped a form, criterion, or assignment, consider what responsibility governs its review.

Ask what would show that an alternative improves the opportunity or choice at issue.

Make room for a fuller account
Culture influences meaning without making people predictable.

Keep personal reflection, individual preferences, and group evidence distinct and connected.

Question a default, hear the person, and examine the routine when it may repeatedly limit access or opportunity.

title: Understanding Meaning Across Communication Differences
audience: All staff, including supervisors and managers
outcomes: Learn to separate the words a person uses from the meaning you infer from context, so you can catch misunderstandings that grow out of communication differences.
Consider pace, silence, directness, and communication channel without assigning cultural types.
Check understanding in a way that preserves dignity and leaves room for disagreement.
Recognize how a preferred communication style may be confused with credibility or competence.
summary: Learn to separate the words a person uses from the meaning you infer from context, so you can catch misunderstandings that grow out of communication differences.
body:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Understanding Meaning Across Communication Differences
Examine what a message means before it becomes a service decision, a workplace judgment, or a rule about who can contribute.
Foundation self-directed learning

What did you hear?
Someone says, “There are several things to consider.” One listener hears reluctance; another hears preparation.

Before reading on, name what was actually said and two possible meanings.

Which question would clarify the response without deciding the speaker’s attitude?

Observation, interpretation, and response
Observation describes the words or action. Interpretation gives it a meaning that may need checking.

Communication draws on context, purpose, relationships, and learned habits; no identity supplies a fixed script.

An appropriate response makes your understanding open to correction.

Considering is not recorded agreement
A person says they will consider a service option. Staff record acceptance because no direct refusal was offered.

The record may then shape next steps that do not reflect the person’s choice.

Ask what remains open and confirm the actual decision before recording it.

Practice: a service choice still open
A person says, “I’ll consider that option.” Staff record acceptance because no direct refusal was offered. What would support an accurate next step?
A. Keep acceptance in the record and ask about details later.
B. Use a brief to decide what the phrase means for this person.
C. Clarify what remains open and confirm the actual decision before recording it.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Context makes a request understandable
“Please look at this soon” may hide the purpose, timing, and kind of response needed.

A newcomer may be judged against expectations that were never explained.

Name the task and relevant conditions so the person can respond to the actual request.

Directness and care can coexist
A precise question may express care for accuracy; a gentle invitation may express care for the contribution.

Neither tone proves the person’s motive or settles the issue.

Ask what concern the message raises and retain the evidence question.

Silence has more than one explanation
A pause may involve thought, missing information, language processing, access, or another reason.

Fast speech is not automatic evidence of preparation, and quietness is not agreement.

Offer a clear question and appropriate response options; ask rather than assign a cultural type.

Check meaning without testing the person
Summarize your understanding and invite correction: “You are considering the option, and timing is still unclear. What did I miss?”

A quick yes to “Do you understand?” may leave the important question unanswered.

Check the exchange and next step without treating clarification as a test of ability.

A qualified answer and a work judgment
An employee gives a careful explanation of conditions affecting a proposal. A supervisor calls the answer unconfident.

The judgment may hide useful analysis and influence later briefing opportunities.

What would clarify the work before treating a style impression as evidence of readiness?

Practice: a careful answer at work
An employee names conditions affecting a proposal. A supervisor calls the answer unconfident and considers withholding a future briefing. What would improve the judgment?
A. Require a more assertive style without examining the conditions.
B. Clarify the task, examine the conditions, and compare relevant work evidence.
C. Give the employee a permanent communication type from their identity.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Feedback should describe the exchange
Name the observed message, its effect on the task, and the change that could help.

“The condition was unclear” gives more useful information than “you are evasive.”

Invite correction and keep a factual disagreement available.

Adapt the channel to the difficulty
A written question beforehand may support consideration; a conversation may reveal a misunderstanding promptly.

Choose an adjustment connected to a stated or observed need, not an identity prediction.

Ask whether it helps without making the new format another universal rule.

A brief can widen your questions
Community briefs may help you consider context, institutional experience, and varied meanings.

They cannot identify this person’s communication style or explain their silence.

Ask about the exchange, hear the answer, and keep room for variation within every community.

Meaning does not establish agreement
You may understand why someone raises a concern and still need to examine the evidence or alternatives.

A calmer exchange is not proof that a decision is accurate or accepted.

Record what is agreed, what remains open, and what the next response actually involves.

Stories and planning questions
Community participants want room to explain experiences. Planners want answers to three specific service questions.

Calling the stories unfocused may silence concerns the questions did not anticipate.

Clarify the purpose and what each approach could contribute before choosing the format.

Practice: hearing stories and questions
Community participants want room for stories; planners want answers to three service questions. Some stories raise issues the questions missed. What would clarify a useful format?
A. Ask what each approach must preserve and consider usable ways to hear both.
B. Treat the stories as unfocused and return only to the prepared questions.
C. Declare agreement because participants and planners both want better services.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

When a style preference becomes a gate
A favored accent, pace, or amount of context can be mistaken for credibility or professional ability.

If that impression shapes recruitment, assignments, and feedback, opportunity may become uneven.

Define the actual requirement and examine relevant evidence through the appropriate responsibility.

Ask what became clearer
A revised explanation can make a condition easier to follow without settling the underlying choice.

Hear whether the person could use it and identify what remains unresolved.

Retain useful progress without claiming everyone now understands or agrees.

Rewrite an exchange
Choose a practice phrase: “unprepared,” “agreed,” or “difficult to work with.”

Replace it with the actual message, your interpretation, and a question that could clarify meaning.

Explain how leaving the label unchanged could affect a later service or workplace decision.

Clear communication is shared work
The person with more institutional knowledge may be able to explain context others cannot infer.

A request for clarification can reveal missing information rather than lack of competence.

Retain necessary standards, accessible arrangements, and the right response to serious concerns.

Keep meaning and evidence connected
Notice the message, check the interpretation, and choose an appropriate response.

Ask how the same habit could affect service choice, workplace opportunity, or community influence if repeated.

Continue learning through community briefs, accessible communication, and intercultural practice.

title: Unconscious Bias
audience: All staff, including supervisors and managers
outcomes: Explain automatic associations, first impressions, and decision shortcuts without treating them as a complete account of behavior.
Separate an observation from a judgment about motivation, credibility, or ability.
Use relevant evidence and transparent criteria to interrupt an assumption.
Identify how repeated individual shortcuts can become a routine that distributes opportunity or burden unevenly.
summary: Examine how assumptions influence DSD services, workplace opportunities and the everyday routines that connect them, so you can recognize bias that works outside of conscious awareness.
body:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Unconscious Bias

Examining how assumptions influence DSD services, workplace opportunities, and the routines that connect them.

Self-directed Foundation learning for all staff

First impressions

A familiar colleague and a newer employee offer service proposals. The newer employee brings community feedback the team has not heard.

Which proposal would you first trust? Before continuing, name the evidence that could change your view.

If familiarity settles the choice, a useful concern may never reach the decision.

What a picture cannot tell us

Appearance, accent, disability, and communication style do not establish competence, motivation, or priorities.

A quick impression can affect how much explanation a person receives or whose work gets considered.

Separate what you observe from what you infer. What evidence does this decision need?

Learning focus

Notice where an assumption enters a service, policy, or workforce decision.

Test the evidence and compare what different responses could cause.

Trace how repeated contact, selection, or development routines can make a barrier persist. Identify what remains unknown.

Practice: a missed service contact

Two service calls went unanswered. A record says the person “does not care.” What response would avoid turning that assumption into a service barrier?

A. Check contact conditions and preferred communication before drawing a conclusion about motivation.

B. Treat the existing label as confirmation that more contact is pointless.

C. Use a culture brief to infer why this person did not respond.

In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Learning at your own pace

Use the practice situations to examine your reasoning privately.

You do not need to disclose personal experiences, test results, or case information.

You can reconsider an answer after reading the feedback. Focus on the decision, its possible effects, and the evidence still needed.

Understanding unconscious bias

Unconscious bias involves associations or assumptions that can influence interpretation without deliberate awareness.

“Implicit bias” often describes related concepts. An association, a decision, and a disparity provide different evidence.

Examine how an impression may shape a decision and its effects; one does not automatically prove the other.

Reflection: a routine decision

A referral calls a person “difficult to contact.” The next staff member considers ending follow-up.

What information would you check before accepting that description?

Compare the possible effects of stopping contact and trying a usable alternative. What still needs to be learned?

Research and everyday practice

Research findings depend on the setting, people studied, and what was measured.

Awareness of bias, decision quality, and service or workplace outcomes are different questions.

Use research to identify a mechanism worth examining. Check the actual decision and local evidence before claiming a pattern.

Bias in human-services work

Assumptions can shape whose concern is heard, what a service record says, and which policy option receives attention.

Listening only to familiar partners may leave an access barrier unexplored.

Ask whose experience is missing, how their input could affect the choice, and what the evidence supports.

Practice: evidence in a policy proposal

A polished service proposal hears only from the team’s usual partners. People facing access barriers are missing. What response would best test the proposal before those barriers are carried forward?

A. Treat clear writing as evidence that the proposal is ready.

B. Apply the relevant criteria, examine missing perspectives, and seek evidence that could challenge the proposal.

C. Reject the proposal because familiar partners contributed.

In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Bias and declared beliefs

An automatic association may differ from a person’s stated values.

Under pressure, a familiar explanation can receive less scrutiny and shape a consequential choice.

Examine criteria, information, and effects. A useful correction does not depend on proving someone intended harm.

Affinity bias

Affinity bias favors people who feel familiar or similar.

Informal invitations may keep recruitment, mentoring, and development within the same circle.

If the pattern repeats, people outside that circle may lack the experience later called “readiness.” How could access be widened?

Confirmation bias

Confirmation bias favors information that supports an existing belief.

A label such as “uncooperative” can make a missed call seem decisive and other explanations easy to overlook.

If the label follows the person, later decisions may repeat the barrier. What evidence could challenge it?

The halo effect

The halo effect lets one favorable impression influence judgments about unrelated qualities.

A polished proposal can seem effective before its evidence, feasibility, and access effects are examined.

If presentation replaces scrutiny, an existing barrier may survive the proposed change. Assess each relevant quality separately.

Perception bias

Perception bias occurs when assumptions about a group shape how behavior is understood.

Quietness may be mistaken for disengagement, or an accent for limited expertise.

If those impressions govern invitations and feedback, a contribution can remain unseen. What evidence would give a fuller account?

Practice: development and advancement

A supervisor offers legislative-analysis assignments to familiar employees, then cites that experience in advancement decisions. What response would help examine and improve this opportunity route?

A. Keep invitations informal because experienced employees are easier to select.

B. Ask employees to disclose personal bias-test results.

C. Clarify opportunities and relevant criteria, then examine who can participate and gain experience.

In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

A decision process we can examine

A team offers development assignments through informal recommendations.

Examine who learns about the work, the criteria used, and the support available to participate.

Early access can shape experience, recognition, advancement, and retention. Trace that sequence before claiming what caused an unequal result.

Practice: observation or assumption?

“Two calls were not returned” records an event. “The person does not care” adds an unsupported claim about motivation.

Rewrite the second note using only what is known. Leave the reason for no response open.

Consider how each version could affect the next staff member’s contact decision.

Practice: fair criteria

A supervisor calls the employee who speaks most in meetings “the most engaged.”

Name two contributions the role actually needs, then consider the evidence for each employee.

When visibility becomes the standard, written analysis or careful follow-through may lose credit and development opportunities.

Practices that reduce avoidable bias

Separate observations from interpretations. Look for evidence that could change the first explanation.

Define relevant criteria before comparing people or proposals, and hear perspectives that test the preferred answer.

Return to the effects: did the revised contact, invitation, or explanation reduce the barrier, and what remains uncertain?

Continuing the learning

Choose a practice service or workforce decision, or a suitable example within your responsibility.

Identify the impression, the decision it could shape, and the barrier or opportunity that might follow. Name the missing evidence.

Use One DSD community briefs, engagement resources, and the Equity Analysis Toolkit to deepen the inquiry.

title: Understanding White Privilege
audience: All staff, including supervisors and managers
outcomes: Explain unearned racial advantage while recognizing effort, hardship, disability, and variation within racial groups.
Identify how established pathways, networks, and expectations may be easier for some people to navigate.
Distinguish a possible racial mechanism from a conclusion requiring further evidence.
Describe a fairer opportunity without asking an affected person to prove the whole concept.
summary: Take a clear, honest look at how racial advantage shows up in DSD service access, workplace culture and institutional practice, and what that means for your work.
body:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Understanding White Privilege

Examining racial advantage in DSD service access, workplace culture, and institutional practice.

Self-directed Foundation learning for all staff

Learning focus

White privilege describes advantages associated with being perceived as white in a society shaped by racial inequality. It can coexist with effort, hardship, and disability.

Trace how an action can affect access or recognition, then ask what happens when the practice repeats.

Use community perspectives and evidence to compare a more equitable response.

Learning with care

Learn at your own pace; the examples are practice.

You do not need to disclose personal harm, defend your identity, or speak for a racial group.

Notice when a familiar practice feels fair to you. What might someone with a different experience need you to examine?

Understanding race

Race is a social category with real consequences for treatment, access, and opportunity.

A racial category cannot establish an individual’s abilities, beliefs, or priorities.

Pause: whose account is readily believed in a service conversation, and what could happen if that judgment becomes a routine?

Practice: hardship and racial advantage

A service participant says, “I have a disability and struggled financially, so racial advantage cannot apply to me.” A colleague suggests setting the racial concern aside. What keeps the inquiry useful?

A. Explain that those hardships are irrelevant.

B. Acknowledge the hardship and examine the specific racial barrier being discussed.

C. Compare everyone’s hardship until the group agrees who struggled most.

In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Understanding ethnicity

Ethnicity can involve heritage, language, traditions, history, and community relationships. It is not interchangeable with race.

Culture briefs provide background and questions, not an individual profile.

Let people describe the identities and preferences relevant to their own situation.

Related ideas

Stereotype: a broad assumption about a group. Prejudice: a group-based judgment or attitude.

Discrimination concerns unequal treatment. Racism involves racial beliefs and practices that sustain unequal treatment or opportunity.

White privilege directs attention to racial advantage, including advantages within ordinary routines.

Individual treatment and systemic patterns

An incident and a repeated institutional pattern need related but distinct inquiry.

Trace the action, its possible effect, and the process that could make it recur.

Address the immediate concern while preserving appropriate reporting options; broader evidence can help examine a racial pattern.

Understanding white privilege

White privilege describes advantages associated with being perceived as white in a society shaped by racial inequality.

A person may benefit without choosing or noticing the advantage.

Ask which racial barrier is less likely to be encountered and which routine could preserve that difference.

Advantages that can go unnoticed

Racial advantage may appear in assumed credibility, representation, established networks, or freedom from stereotypes.

A familiar route to information can become a route to experience and influence.

Ask who can use that route and what evidence would clarify a racial pattern.

Practice: access across employment

A development assignment reaches an informal circle before other employees hear about it. Later, that experience supports advancement. What is established?

A. The invitation created unequal access to information; a racial pattern requires further evidence.

B. The example alone proves which racial groups benefited and why.

C. There is no inequity unless someone intended to exclude others.

In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Reflection: access to opportunity

A development opportunity reaches a familiar circle before other employees hear about it.

The information gap is visible. A racial pattern needs evidence about access, selection, and relevant circumstances.

Trace the path from invitation to experience, recognition, advancement, and retention.

The effect of an ordinary practice

A service process assumes people can find information, interpret unfamiliar terms, and obtain help through established contacts.

Those assumptions may place extra effort or delay on people outside familiar networks.

Whose experience would help examine a racial barrier, and how could the process change in response?

Advantage and hardship

Racial advantage can coexist with poverty, disability, loss, and other hardship.

Effort and hardship matter; they do not settle whether a particular racial barrier also exists.

Keep the specific service or workforce practice in view instead of ranking people’s lives.

Practice: whose voice receives credit?

A colleague of color raises a policy concern. It receives attention only after a white colleague repeats it.

Acknowledge the original contribution and invite the colleague’s own explanation.

Consider how repeated losses of credit could affect influence, development, and advancement.

A response in the moment

“That returns to the concern our colleague raised earlier. Let’s hear their perspective.”

Restore credit now; examine the pattern with relevant evidence.

Support through everyday practice

Listen to the concern and recognize the contribution or barrier described.

Make opportunities and criteria understandable, restore credit, and examine who can participate.

Ask whether changing the routine could prevent the same barrier from recurring.

Practice: community knowledge and influence

People affected by a service change raise racial access concerns. The team responds only after a familiar professional repeats them. What would help?

A. Ask participants to disclose personal harm before considering the concern.

B. Move on because the concern was eventually discussed.

C. Recognize the original contribution, invite clarification, and examine how the team assigns credibility.

In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Learning and follow-through

Choose a specific service or workforce practice and identify what remains unknown.

Use culture briefs to prepare questions and hear from people affected.

The Equity Analysis Toolkit can help compare evidence, racial barriers, alternatives, and a supported next step.

Practice: a fairer invitation

An open development notice replaces informal invitations, but employees still find its criteria unclear.

Distribution is only one part of access; unclear criteria can preserve the original advantage.

What explanation and follow-up would help show whether people previously overlooked can use the opportunity?

Continuing the learning

Choose a service or employee-life-cycle practice for closer examination.

Describe an action, its possible barrier or advantage, and what repetition could sustain.

Keep race visible alongside disability and other circumstances; use community knowledge and evidence to consider a useful response.

title: Microaggressions: Recognizing Messages and Responding with Care
audience: All staff, including supervisors and managers
outcomes: Learn to recognize how an everyday comment can communicate exclusion or diminished credibility based on identity, and how to respond with care when it happens.
Hold stated intent and reported impact together without requiring agreement about motive.
Choose a proportionate response that respects the affected person’s preferences.
Notice when repeated messages reinforce an expectation about who belongs or is considered capable.
summary: Learn to recognize how an everyday comment can communicate exclusion or diminished credibility based on identity, and how to respond with care when it happens.
body:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Microaggressions: Recognizing Messages and Responding with Care
Recognize identity-based messages, respond with care, and examine how recurring interactions can shape service and workplace opportunity.
Foundation self-directed learning

Listen to the message inside the comment
“You are surprisingly knowledgeable” sounds positive, yet the surprise suggests a low expectation.

What part describes the contribution? What part compares the person with an unstated expectation?

Consider context before deciding what the comment communicates.

What the term helps us notice
A microaggression is an everyday verbal, behavioral, or environmental message that can communicate identity-based exclusion or diminished standing.

“Micro” describes the everyday scale, not a guaranteed small effect.

Not every discourtesy is identity-based; explain the connection rather than rushing to a label.

Speaking past the person receiving services
An adult asks about a service option. Staff answer the accompanying support person and never return to the adult.

The exchange may communicate that the adult’s voice counts less. If routine, it can shape plans around others’ accounts.

Ask the person how they want to communicate and involve support.

Hear the person without dismissing support
An adult asks about a service option. Staff repeatedly answer the accompanying support person. The adult asks to be addressed directly. What is the most useful next response?
A. Continue through the support person because that seems easier.
B. Address the adult and ask how they want support involved.
C. Exclude the support person from all future conversations.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Intent and impact answer different questions
Intent concerns what the speaker meant. Impact concerns what the exchange did or communicated.

A good intention does not erase a reported effect. A reported effect does not reveal every motive.

Acknowledge the specific action before defending your intention.

Repetition changes the experience
One question about background may be welcome. Repeatedly rejecting a person’s answer can communicate that it does not count.

The listener may notice one exchange while the recipient recognizes a recurring pattern.

Ask about context without demanding a public history of harm.

A response can increase or reduce agency
A brief interruption, a private check-in, or an appropriate formal route may each fit a different situation.

Do not make the affected person explain an identity, confront someone, or accept an apology.

Consider your role, immediate safety, and the person’s wishes.

Praise the work without the stereotype
Specific feedback names the analysis, explanation, or contribution that helped.

Surprise about a person’s language or ability may make identity the comparison instead.

Try rewriting “surprisingly articulate” as useful feedback about the work.

When an employee’s contribution disappears
A new employee identifies a missing service address. A colleague comments on their “unexpectedly good English”; discussion moves away from the address.

The comment can position the employee as an outsider while leaving useful work unanswered.

Return credit and attention to the actual contribution.

Return to the contribution
A new employee identifies a missing service address. A colleague says their English is “unexpectedly good,” and the discussion moves on. What response best preserves their contribution?
A. Tell the employee it was a compliment and ask them to move on.
B. Ask the employee to teach everyone about their community.
C. Name the useful address question, address the assumption, and offer a private check-in.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Repair a consequence, not just a sentence
An apology can acknowledge an action without demanding forgiveness.

If credit, wording, or an opportunity was affected, consider the appropriate correction.

Repair is more credible when the relevant behavior changes.

Credibility can travel through the life cycle
Repeated identity-based surprise may shape whose expertise is recognized, who receives visible assignments, and whose work is credited.

Examine the actual decision and criteria rather than inferring ability from identity.

A supportive exchange should not become a new requirement to prove belonging.

Use a brief without making a person the lesson
A community brief can prepare attention to history, institutions, and communication context.

It cannot establish how a particular comment affected an individual.

Invite varied accounts without asking one employee or participant to represent a whole community.

Environmental messages also communicate
Images, examples, and introductions can suggest who belongs without a direct remark.

A narrow pattern of representation may leave some people’s lives outside the expected picture.

Review the purpose and recurring choices; one image alone does not explain every effect.

An invitation to speak for everyone
At a listening session, staff ask the only participant from one community to explain what “their people” need.

The request can make participation a burden of representation and leave other experiences unheard.

Ask about the person’s own chosen perspective and seek additional voices.

Invite a perspective without assigning representation
At a listening session, staff ask the only participant from one community to explain what “their people” need. What would make the invitation more respectful and useful?
A. Invite their chosen perspective and seek varied accounts through usable participation routes.
B. Record their answer as the position of the whole community.
C. Avoid community perspectives altogether to prevent assumptions.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Support and formal responsibilities remain distinct
A learning conversation can offer support; it does not decide whether conduct meets a legal or workplace standard.

Use current agency reporting routes and the responsibilities of your actual role.

An apology, course result, or consultant conversation must not become a gate to an applicable process.

Look for the routine that carries the message
A repeated introduction, attribution habit, or speaking rule can make the same exclusion easier to reproduce.

Ask which routine connects the message with a decision or opportunity.

Changing the routine can matter even when no one’s complete motive is known.

Rewrite the response in your own words
Choose the practice language compliment or service conversation.

Name the specific action, explain a possible effect, and write a proportionate response.

What would remain unknown after that response? Your reflection can stay private.

Notice what changes after the reply
A changed comment, corrected record, or revised introduction is an action you can identify.

Understanding its effect requires relevant feedback and attention to the recurring practice.

No later response does not mean agreement, forgiveness, or proof that the concern was minor.

Keep dignity and accurate recognition together
Recognize the message in context, retain choice, and address the consequence you can understand.

Recurring interactions deserve attention to the routine as well as the words.

Continue with bias, belonging, and community engagement resources when they help deepen the question.

title: Race, Disability, and Overlapping Barriers
audience: All staff, including supervisors and managers
outcomes: Intersectionality is about how conditions such as race and disability interact, not a list or ranking of identities. This course explains how those overlapping barriers combine in people’s lives.
Identify how separate support processes may miss a combined barrier.
Ask what information could clarify a difference in experience without assuming its cause.
Consider an improvement that addresses access and racial equity together.
summary: Intersectionality is about how conditions such as race and disability interact, not a list or ranking of identities. This course explains how those overlapping barriers combine in people’s lives.
body:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Race, Disability, and Overlapping Barriers
Examine how racial expectations, disability access, and institutional arrangements can interact in services and workplace opportunity.
Foundation self-directed learning

When two good supports do not connect
An accessible English document and an inaccessible translated image are offered as separate options.

A reader needs both the translated language and screen-reader access. Neither version meets the combined need.

What would a review of each feature alone miss?

Intersectionality examines interacting power
Intersectionality asks how interacting forms of power and exclusion can disappear in a single-category explanation.

Its origins include Kimberlé Crenshaw’s examination of Black women’s experiences within race and sex discrimination frameworks.

It is more than listing identities or adding up disadvantage.

Reach the invitation and use it
A service discussion offers access support, but invitations circulate only through a familiar English-language network.

People outside that network may never reach the supported event. Repeating the route can narrow whose needs shape planning.

Examine outreach and participation together, using varied accounts.

Follow the whole participation route
A service discussion offers access support. Invitations circulate only through a familiar English-language network, and few perspectives reach planning. What is the best starting response?
A. Declare participation equitable because access support was offered.
B. Assume every absent racial community has the same reason for not attending.
C. Examine outreach and response routes together with varied, voluntarily offered accounts.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Identity is not the problem to repair
A racial or disability identity does not explain a barrier by itself.

Ask which requirement, assumption, resource, or decision makes the activity harder to access.

Keep strengths, preferences, and agency in the account.

Follow where the difference is produced
Finding information, responding, being assessed, and receiving a result are connected steps.

A barrier at an early step can change who appears in later information.

Ask which point needs examination before attaching a cause to the final difference.

Separate processes can leave a shared gap
One area may arrange access support while another handles outreach or response forms.

Each task can look successful while the combined route remains unusable.

State where the supports meet so the appropriate people can examine them together.

Do not turn complexity into a ranking
No identity inventory can calculate a person’s hardship or predict their choices.

A person can encounter a barrier in one setting and have an advantage in another.

Ask about the task and necessary information without demanding a personal biography.

Access to training is not access to opportunity
An employee can use the training room, yet project leads choose mentees through a familiar informal network.

Racial expectations and inaccessible networking arrangements may interact in who receives development opportunities.

Examine the criteria, invitation routes, and employee’s account before deciding why.

Training access and mentoring access
An employee can use the training room but does not reach informal mentoring opportunities. Racial expectations and inaccessible networking may be relevant. What response best examines the concern?
A. Inspect opportunity criteria, invitation routes, and the employee’s chosen account together.
B. Conclude that physical room access proves equal development opportunity.
C. Attribute the outcome to the employee’s identities without examining the process.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Look across relevant life-cycle decisions
Recruitment, onboarding, assignments, development, and advancement may use different routes to opportunity.

An early access barrier or credibility judgment can influence a later decision.

Trace the connection that matters; do not assume every stage works the same way.

A group difference is a question, not a verdict
A difference in outcomes can justify careful inquiry without establishing its cause.

Ask who is included, what the denominator describes, and whether information is comparable.

Small or incomplete categories may conceal variation and uncertainty.

Prepare with briefs, then hear varied experience
Community briefs can introduce history, institutions, and relevant questions.

They cannot establish how race and disability combine for a particular person.

Invite perspectives that do not fit a single category, without requiring disclosure or representation.

Test whether the supports work together
Consider the actual document, invitation, response route, and activity a person will use.

Improving one feature may leave another barrier intact.

A joined-up proposal is a useful beginning; effectiveness still needs appropriate checks and feedback.

An accessible invitation leads to a closed route
A community invitation is translated and accessible. Its registration form requires English, and access requests are available only after registration.

The sequence can exclude people before support is arranged.

Examine the whole route and ask which alternatives would be usable.

Supports separated by the registration step
An accessible translated invitation leads to an English-only registration form. Access requests become available only after registration. Which response best addresses the connected barrier?
A. Provide more copies of the same invitation.
B. Review registration and support timing together, seeking usable alternatives and appropriate feedback.
C. Mark translation and access complete because each exists somewhere in the process.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Distinguish explanation from accusation
You can identify a possible barrier without deciding anyone’s complete motive.

Describe the action, its plausible effect, and the evidence that would test the connection.

Clear questions make a concern easier to examine without weakening its importance.

Keep the person’s whole experience visible
One office’s completed task is not the same as a person’s usable experience.

Listen for where transitions between supports create difficulty.

Preserve the person’s chosen priorities rather than deciding that staff coordination is their main goal.

Rewrite a single-category explanation
Take the practice training or registration case.

Write what a disability-only or race-only account might notice and miss.

Then describe an interacting condition, a better question, and one limit of the evidence.

Compare a change with the original barrier
Ask whether the proposed response addresses the connection that caused difficulty.

Consider whether the change shifts a burden to another step or another group.

Retain missing information rather than treating silence as success.

Ask about the interaction that matters
Intersectional thinking examines conditions and power people experience together.

Keep identity, agency, evidence, and uncertainty distinct.

Continue with accessibility, racial equity, community engagement, and data resources as the question requires.

title: Disability, Rights, Identity, and Belonging
audience: All staff, including supervisors and managers
outcomes: Compare medical, social, cultural and rights-based ways of understanding disability, and consider how each one shapes questions of identity, rights and belonging.
Recognize how a deficit description can obscure a person’s strengths and the surrounding barriers.
Distinguish an individual support need from a condition the organization can change.
Respect disability identity without expecting any person to represent all disabled people.
summary: Compare medical, social, cultural and rights-based ways of understanding disability, and consider how each one shapes questions of identity, rights and belonging.
body:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Disability, Rights, Identity, and Belonging
Understand disability through more than limitations, and examine the conditions that shape participation in services and work.
Foundation self-directed learning

Who is described as the problem?
“The person cannot complete our form” directs attention toward the person.

“The form requires handwriting in small boxes” makes a design condition visible.

What could each description lead the next reader to do?

Several perspectives answer different questions
A medical view asks about a condition or treatment. A social view asks what restricts participation in the environment.

Functional, rights-based, cultural, and intersectional views add questions about activity, entitlement, identity, and interacting barriers.

No single view describes the whole person.

A program description can narrow possibility
A page describes people chiefly as unable to manage ordinary life and says staff decide what is best.

The wording may obscure strengths, chosen support, and decision-making. Repetition can normalize low expectations.

Describe the purpose and support accurately while retaining agency and any required terms.

Describe support without erasing agency
A public page describes people chiefly as unable to manage life and says staff decide what is best. Which revision best improves the account without denying support needs?
A. Replace every legal or program term immediately with positive language.
B. Describe the support purpose, people’s priorities, and relevant conditions, retaining required terms for review.
C. Keep the description because people who need support cannot direct decisions.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Keep health and support needs visible
Barrier removal should not erase pain, fatigue, communication needs, or other experiences a person chooses to describe.

Ask what helps with this activity rather than requesting unnecessary medical detail.

Actual care and formal processes retain their own responsibilities.

Describe activity in context
A functional question asks what the person can do in a particular setting, with relevant supports.

Ability is not a fixed verdict derived from one difficult task.

Changing the tool, pace, or environment may change what becomes possible.

Rights are more than a charitable response
A rights-based view asks about access, equal opportunity, participation, and the responsibilities of the relevant process.

A helpful intention is not the same as an appropriate rights-based response.

Use the responsible agency routes for actual rights, service, or accommodation questions.

Disability can also be identity and culture
Disability communities include histories, languages, arts, humor, organizing, and varied views about access.

Some people understand disability as central to identity; others describe it differently.

Do not assume that a medical category tells you the person’s chosen meaning.

Onboarding: separate the task from the default
A new employee asks for an accessible training format. A colleague treats the request as evidence the role may be unsuitable.

That inference can turn a design gap into a capability judgment before the work is examined.

Clarify the task, access barrier, and appropriate support process.

An access request during onboarding
A new employee requests an accessible training format. A colleague says this shows the role may not fit. What is the most useful response?
A. Clarify the task and format barrier, then use the appropriate access process without assuming capability.
B. Reduce future assignments because the employee has already shown a limitation.
C. Promise every requested change without examining the task or relevant process.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Language preferences belong to people
Person-first and identity-first language can each be meaningful in different contexts.

Ask and follow a person’s preference when appropriate; do not impose one universal rule.

Required legal wording and general public writing may need different review.

Belonging includes opportunity to contribute
Welcoming language matters, but participation also depends on usable arrangements and recognition of expertise.

Consider access to assignments, learning, feedback, and advancement where relevant.

A friendly interaction does not establish that the whole employee experience is accessible.

Interdependence can support self-direction
People commonly rely on relationships, tools, and shared knowledge to pursue their goals.

Using support does not automatically remove agency or make a person’s priorities less important.

Ask how the person wants support involved rather than equating independence with doing everything alone.

Learn with self-advocates and varied communities
Community briefs can prepare questions about history, access, and institutional experience.

Self-advocates bring expertise that a description of needs alone may miss.

Invite varied, voluntary perspectives without assigning representation by disability or other identity.

Do not reduce engagement to a personal story
A planning group asks one disabled participant to share an inspiring story rather than comment on the service design.

The request can replace practical expertise with a familiar narrative and leave the design question unanswered.

Invite the person’s chosen contribution to an open question.

Invite expertise rather than an inspiration story
At a service-design session, a disabled participant is asked to share an inspiring personal story instead of commenting on the form under review. Which invitation is better?
A. Ask them to represent every disabled person’s needs.
B. Remove the participant from the review because lived experience is not technical expertise.
C. Invite their chosen observations about the form, with usable participation and no required personal disclosure.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

A deficit frame can travel into decisions
A broad description of inability may be copied into notes, templates, and planning assumptions.

Future readers may offer fewer choices without examining the original conditions.

Keep the account specific and identify the barrier that could be reviewed.

Support today and design for the next person
An immediate alternative can help with the present task. A design review can reduce the need to request the same workaround repeatedly.

Neither response guarantees every access need is met.

Ask whether the person can use the actual arrangement and what remains difficult.

Rewrite a description without losing the need
Use the practice form, program description, or training example.

Retain the relevant support need, restore the person’s agency, and name a changeable condition.

What would a later reader understand differently? No personal record is needed.

A new perspective is not a completed finding
Recognizing a barrier or reframing a sentence is a meaningful learning step.

An approved change, usable support, and improved experience each need their own evidence.

Missing feedback leaves a question open; it does not establish success or failure.

Keep the whole person in view
Disability perspectives can reveal support needs, rights, identity, expertise, and environmental barriers together.

Use the lens that clarifies the question without turning it into a complete description of someone.

Continue with accessibility, person-centered thinking, and community engagement when useful.

title: Accessibility in Everyday Services and Work
audience: All staff, including supervisors and managers
outcomes: Learn to spot physical, digital, communication and participation barriers in ordinary activities, from the everyday services people use to the routine tasks of your own work.
Ask about access without demanding unnecessary personal information.
Consider accessible choices before requiring someone to request an exception.
Explain how a recurring inaccessible default shifts effort and delay onto the person seeking access.
summary: Learn to spot physical, digital, communication and participation barriers in ordinary activities, from the everyday services people use to the routine tasks of your own work.
body:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Accessibility in Everyday Services and Work
Notice access barriers, consider usable alternatives, and reduce recurring effort and delay in services, learning, and participation.
Foundation self-directed learning

A door opens, but the route stops
An accessible entrance leads to a meeting where the essential handout is an unreadable image.

Physical entry does not establish access to the discussion.

Where would you examine the route from arrival to meaningful participation?

Design and individual support work together
Accessible design anticipates recurring barriers before someone has to request a change.

Individual support responds to needs that a general design may not fully meet.

Neither is a reason to ignore the other; actual processes and responsibilities remain.

The same information in a usable form
A public presentation explains service choices, but its handout is a scanned image and the speaker reads quickly.

Some participants may miss information needed to compare options. Repetition can narrow whose preferences shape the discussion.

Offer usable formats and pace, then ask about remaining barriers.

Information distributed is not information usable
A public service meeting uses a scanned handout and a fast spoken explanation. Some participants cannot use the information to compare choices. What is the best response?
A. Offer the same file again and say the information was already provided.
B. Consider usable formats and pace, then check remaining barriers through appropriate questions.
C. Assume that everyone needs one identical alternative format.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Digital access includes how a task works
A form may look clear yet require a mouse, rely on color alone, or lack meaningful labels.

People use different technologies and ways of navigating.

Examine the task with appropriate access checks; appearance alone cannot establish usability.

Documents need structure and meaning
Clear headings, readable text, meaningful links, and alternatives for useful images can support understanding and navigation.

A scan or decorative layout may hide the structure.

Keep essential meaning available and check the actual file people receive.

Audio and video require usable alternatives
Captions, transcripts, and descriptions can make different parts of media available.

Automatic output may omit names, meaning, or important visual information.

Review the relevant content rather than treating the existence of an alternative as proof it works.

Meeting access begins before the meeting
An understandable invitation, usable materials, clear purpose, and ways to contribute affect who can prepare and participate.

Ask about the activity and support without demanding unnecessary personal details.

Time, pace, breaks, and response routes may also matter.

Onboarding through a single unavailable format
A new employee receives essential instructions only in an inaccessible recording. They ask for usable information but are told to learn by watching others.

That can shift extra effort onto the employee and leave gaps in starting work.

Examine the actual information and provide an appropriate usable route.

Essential onboarding information
A new employee cannot use the only recording containing essential instructions. Staff suggest watching colleagues informally. Which response best addresses the barrier?
A. Clarify the missing information and arrange a usable route through the appropriate process.
B. Treat the employee’s slower start as evidence they lack initiative.
C. Wait for the employee to disclose a diagnosis before considering any information format.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Access affects more than the first day
Recurring formats and meeting arrangements can shape access to feedback, development, assignments, and advancement.

A request should not automatically become a capability judgment.

Examine the opportunity and the conditions that make it usable.

Ask before helping
An offer of help should leave the person free to accept, decline, or explain a preferred method.

Speak to the person and allow their communication time and chosen support.

Useful intent does not establish that an unasked intervention helps.

A brief prepares questions about access
Community briefs can prompt attention to language, institutional experience, and varied participation conditions.

They do not identify an individual’s access needs.

Combine informed preparation with direct, appropriate questions and varied community feedback.

The response route is part of participation
A clear invitation can still lead to an unusable registration form or a voice-only contact route.

People may leave before they can request support.

Review the connected steps and consider alternatives through the appropriate responsibilities.

The invitation asks people to call only
A community session lists one voice telephone number for registration and access questions.

A participant explains that they cannot use that route. Staff respond that help is available after registration.

Which response would examine the gate rather than repeat it?

Help beyond an unusable registration gate
A community invitation lists only a voice telephone number. A participant cannot use that route and is told support is available after registration. What should staff consider?
A. Mark the session accessible because help was advertised.
B. Use a culture brief to infer what the participant needs without asking.
C. Examine a usable response route and access timing, informed by the participant’s account.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
