Focus on the relevant contribution rather than making identity the test of capability.

Three ways to respond in the moment
Clarification asks what supports an assumption. A brief boundary names a needed change. Redirection restores the contribution or task.

Choose the response that fits the purpose, setting, and role. No sentence works everywhere.

Role, safety, and the person’s choices
Consider your role, the setting, and whether a response could increase unwanted attention. Appropriate help or a later response may fit.

Uncertainty about perfect wording does not require doing nothing. Preserve the person’s choices while addressing what you can responsibly change.

An idea repeated without credit
A colleague’s policy suggestion is interrupted and later repeated as someone else’s idea. Returning credit and offering the turn can restore the contribution.

If this recurs, examine how meeting and recognition practices influence development opportunities.

Practice: an idea loses its author
A colleague’s policy proposal is interrupted, then repeated as someone else’s idea. You heard the original contribution. Which response best restores it?
A. Deliver a long explanation of workplace exclusion before the proposal is discussed.
B. Identify the colleague’s original proposal and offer them room to finish if they wish.
C. Tell the colleague privately that the group probably meant well.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Support without taking over
Offer a specific choice: “Would a follow-up from me be useful?” or “Would you prefer some space?”

The person may want another response or none. An offer does not authorize sharing their account or deciding their preferred outcome.

Informal support and actual responsibilities
A supportive conversation differs from an established reporting or review process. Follow the responsibilities that apply to your role.

Do not wait for agreement on the term microaggression, an apology, or consultant guidance when an actual duty requires action.

Information shared for a purpose
Describe what you heard or saw accurately if the appropriate process needs it. Avoid adding inferred motives or invented details.

An offer of support is not permission to record, circulate, or publish another person’s experience.

Community perspectives on support
People may differ about whether a public correction, private support, or another response is useful.

Culture briefs can prepare thoughtful questions. They do not decide what someone must find harmful or how they must respond.

An assignment based on appearance
A community contributor is asked to interpret because staff infer a language from appearance. Their skills, interest, and role have not been checked.

Return to the actual language arrangements and staffing requirements without demanding a personal identity explanation.

Practice: an unverified language assignment
A community contributor is asked to interpret because staff infer a language from appearance. Skills, interest, and role have not been checked. What response best corrects the assumption?
A. Ask the contributor to list their ancestry and languages in front of the group.
B. Keep the assignment because staff were trying to recognize a useful identity.
C. Return to appropriate language arrangements and confirmed role information without an identity demand.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Repeated exclusions and the routine behind them
Repeated interruption, lost credit, or identity-based assignments can shape whose work is visible and whose knowledge influences decisions.

Examine the meeting, assignment, and recognition practices that make the action easier to repeat.

Evidence for a limited improvement
A corrected note can show that credit was restored. It does not prove everyone had a chance to contribute or that exclusion ended.

Use specific observations and appropriate optional feedback. Missing responses remain unknown.

Opportunity across the employee life cycle
Recruitment, onboarding, supervision, development, and retention involve who is heard, trusted, credited, and given opportunity.

Repeated subtle exclusion may affect those choices. Examine the relevant actions and consequences rather than relying only on intent.

Writing a response with a clear purpose
Privately write a brief reply for a practice exchange. Choose whether to clarify, set a boundary, or restore a contribution.

Explain what the response could change, what it could add to the burden, and what would still be unresolved.

Purposeful responses and continuing care
Address the specific assumption or displaced contribution. Preserve choice and follow actual responsibilities.

Consider a fitting support offer without taking control of the person’s story.

Examine repeated practices and their evidence before claiming the broader problem is resolved.

title: Racial Advantage and the Everyday Gates to Opportunity
audience: All staff; supervisor focus when examining access to work opportunities.
outcomes: Racial advantage can coexist with disability, financial hardship or other barriers. This course explains how that works and how it plays out at the everyday gates to opportunity.
Trace how familiar networks and credibility judgments influence access to information and opportunity.
Compare a stated merit standard with the opportunities people had to demonstrate it.
Develop a supported improvement without assuming that every difference proves racial discrimination.
summary: Racial advantage can coexist with disability, financial hardship or other barriers. This course explains how that works and how it plays out at the everyday gates to opportunity.
body:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Racial Advantage and the Everyday Gates to Opportunity
Examining how everyday information, credibility, and opportunity can create or sustain racial advantages in DSD services and work.
Intermediate self-directed learning

Effort and enabling conditions
Effort concerns what a person does. Enabling conditions concern what makes that effort possible or easier to recognize.

Privately examine an opportunity in a practice example. Which parts depend on work, and which depend on access to information or support?

White privilege and individual variation
White privilege concerns advantages attached to being treated as white in a particular setting. It is not a claim that a person has never struggled.

Race, disability, income, role, and other circumstances may affect the same pathway in different ways.

Service information through familiar organizations
A service opportunity is announced mainly through established organizations. Staff assume everyone who needs it will hear.

Examining the routes and who could use them may reveal an information gap before familiarity becomes an unstated access condition.

Practice: information through familiar routes
A service opportunity is announced mainly through established organizations. Staff assume everyone was reached, but have no evidence of that. What would best examine access?
A. Trace who could find and use the information, and consider additional appropriate routes.
B. Treat a narrow contact list as proof that every organizer intended racial exclusion.
C. Keep the route because established partners are trusted and no one complained.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Information as an ordinary advantage
Advance notice, explanations, and trusted contacts can make a process easier to enter. People without those routes may appear less prepared.

Identify what information is consequential and whether intended people can obtain it through a usable route.

Networks and their limits
Relationships often connect similar people. This pattern can reflect available contacts as well as preferences.

Examine the opportunity route rather than monitor private friendships. Similarity alone does not establish exclusion or motive.

Credibility and the benefit of the doubt
Familiarity may supply confidence before work evidence is examined. Other people may repeatedly face extra scrutiny.

Compare the relevant standard, the information available, and how uncertainty is interpreted across comparable accounts.

Experience made possible by opportunity
Assignments can create the evidence later used to judge readiness. Unequal entry can therefore reproduce itself.

Distinguish a role that genuinely requires prior experience from an opportunity intended to develop that experience.

An acting assignment that becomes readiness
An acting assignment is offered through an informal conversation. That experience later becomes evidence of promotion readiness.

Review notice, preparation, selection, support, and credit. The final comparison cannot explain who had a chance to build its evidence.

Practice: experience from an informal assignment
An acting assignment was offered through an informal conversation. Its experience is later cited as promotion readiness. What would best examine the opportunity pathway?
A. Ignore the person’s demonstrated work because the original route was informal.
B. Review notice, criteria, access, support, and the work evidence through the appropriate process.
C. Use the final participant’s identity alone to decide why the assignment was made.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Visibility and actual contribution
Work seen in a room is only part of the work a team may contribute. Availability to be seen should not automatically become evidence of capability.

Examine the actual task, information, and contribution through the appropriate work arrangements.

A usable route to an opportunity
Relevant information, an understandable invitation, and appropriate preparation can widen access. The selection standard remains important.

A public announcement helps only if people can find, understand, and use it in time to participate.

Community engagement beyond one familiar partner
Different community voices can reveal missing information routes and practical access conditions.

Culture briefs can prepare questions about communication and relationships. One partner’s familiarity or approval does not establish that everyone was reached.

Access after the invitation
Entering an opportunity does not guarantee useful support, influence, or recognition. Examine what happens after selection.

A broader participant mix may reveal a changed route without proving that every condition became equitable.

A community invitation with unseen gaps
A revised announcement reaches more organizations, but some participants say the language and format remain difficult to use.

Recognize the wider route and examine the remaining access concern. Neither improvement nor unresolved difficulty cancels the other.

Practice: a wider route with a remaining barrier
An announcement reaches more organizations. Some community participants say its language and format remain difficult. What does the evidence support?
A. The wider contact list proves the service information is now equitable.
B. The remaining difficulty means the wider route achieved nothing.
C. The route widened, while usability remains a separate concern needing examination.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

The mechanism that can repeat
Private notice can lead to preparation, preparation to selection, and selection to experience later treated as merit.

If access to those steps follows a racialized pattern, advantage can persist without every participant intending it.

Evidence about the pathway
Examine announcement routes, criteria, opportunities to express interest, support, selection, and consequences.

Use authorized information and relevant expertise. Avoid private racial inventories, friendship monitoring, or required stories of discrimination.

The employee life cycle and accumulated access
Recruitment, onboarding, supervision, development, and retention create repeated opportunities for knowledge and recognition.

Consider where an early advantage becomes a later qualification, and where a more usable route could preserve a fair standard.

Rewriting an opportunity explanation
Privately revise: “They are ready because they have done it before.” Identify how the experience was obtained and what the task truly requires.

Describe one feasible access improvement, its possible effect, and evidence that could challenge your explanation.

Opportunity that can be understood and examined
Recognize effort while examining racial barriers and enabling conditions. Keep identity distinct from a character verdict.

Trace access to information, credibility, experience, support, and recognition.

Choose a supported response and keep its effects and remaining uncertainties visible.

title: Receiving Feedback About Bias and Making a Useful Repair
audience: All staff; useful for supervisors receiving concerns about their decisions.
outcomes: When someone raises a specific concern about bias, learn to listen without turning the conversation into a defense of your character, and then make a useful repair.
Clarify the action and its effect without cross-examining the person.
Offer an apology and a practical change proportionate to what happened.
Recognize recurring feedback as a reason to examine practice, while keeping privacy and formal duties intact.
summary: When someone raises a specific concern about bias, learn to listen without turning the conversation into a defense of your character, and then make a useful repair.
body:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Receiving Feedback About Bias and Making a Useful Repair
Hearing a specific concern, examining your part, and making a useful repair without asking the person to manage your reaction.
Intermediate self-directed learning

The action and the feeling it brings
A concern about one phrase or decision may feel like a judgment of your whole character. Those are different questions.

Privately consider your first reaction to difficult feedback. What would help you return attention to the specific action?

Discomfort and the evidence
Discomfort establishes that the message is difficult to receive. It does not establish whether the factual concern is true or false.

Examine the wording, decision, or interaction. A respectful response can include both accountability and a precise factual disagreement.

A service explanation that assigns blame
A participant says a draft makes families seem irresponsible. Staff want to reply that the intention was to encourage action.

Examine the sentence and its implied explanation. An intention to help does not settle whether the wording adds unsupported blame.

Practice: a sentence about families
A community participant says a service draft describes families as irresponsible when a step is incomplete. Staff want to defend their intention. What response would best examine the concern?
A. Acknowledge the wording, examine what it establishes, and preserve the actual requirement without unsupported blame.
B. Ask the participant to reassure staff that the intention was good before considering a revision.
C. Remove every requirement from the explanation so that nobody feels criticized.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

An opening that keeps the concern available
Name the specific concern before explaining yourself. Invite clarification only where it is needed.

“I hear that the sentence assigns a motive we have not established” offers a more useful opening than a defense of good intentions.

Clarification and cross-examination
A relevant question helps identify what needs correction. Cross-examination seeks to defeat the person offering feedback.

Ask only for information needed to understand the particular concern. Do not demand a complete history before examining a visible issue.

A factual correction that preserves responsibility
You may disagree with one detail and still own another part of the action. Be precise about both.

“I did not draft the sentence, but I approved its use” keeps the fact and the responsibility together.

Different standards in performance feedback
An employee says their work was judged against a standard not applied to comparable work. The supervisor needs specific evidence and relevant criteria.

Receive the concern, examine the comparison, and follow the appropriate review responsibility without treating the complaint as disloyalty.

Apology and practical repair
An apology names the action and the part you own. A repair addresses its effect on a record, decision, or opportunity.

Keep the response proportionate and feasible. Forgiveness and reassurance are not conditions for making a needed correction.

Practice: a different performance standard
An employee says comparable work received different performance feedback. The supervisor finds the concern uncomfortable. What is the most useful next response?
A. Explain how much the supervisor values fairness and ask the employee to withdraw the concern.
B. Receive the specific concern and compare the relevant work, criteria, and feedback through the appropriate process.
C. Accept every interpretation immediately so the employee knows the concern was heard.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

The audience and the person’s privacy
A public error may need a correction for the original audience. A private account should not be repeated to make the apology more convincing.

Ask about a response that identifies the person, while keeping the actual responsibility to correct information clear.

The person can choose a different response
A person may say more, correct your understanding, ask for another route, or decline discussion. Receive that answer without assigning a motive.

Silence does not prove forgiveness, approval, dissatisfaction, or refusal to cooperate.

Community feedback and a useful report-back
Different community accounts can reveal concerns staff did not anticipate. Explain how relevant input was considered and what remains open.

Culture briefs support preparation, but they do not prescribe the meaning of an apology or a person’s response.

A public correction and a private account
A community contributor’s idea is credited incorrectly in a shared summary. They describe the concern privately.

Correct the attribution for the relevant audience without retelling the personal account. Consider how future summaries can preserve accurate credit.

Follow-through after the first reaction
Check whether the promised correction occurred and whether the relevant practice changed. A convincing apology is not the same evidence.

Offer an appropriate update without seeking praise or repeatedly asking the person to confirm your growth.

Practice: correcting credit without retelling
A shared summary credits a community contributor’s idea to someone else. The contributor describes the concern privately. What repair best fits the available evidence?
A. Publish the private conversation to demonstrate that staff understand the harm.
B. Wait to correct the summary until the contributor accepts a public apology.
C. Correct the attribution for the relevant audience without repeating the private account, and examine future checking.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

When defensiveness becomes a repeated barrier
If concerns routinely receive dismissal, extra proof demands, or reputation judgments, people may stop raising useful information.

The absence of complaints then cannot establish fairness. Examine how concerns were received and what responses followed.

A response proportionate to the evidence
One account can identify a specific concern without explaining every cause. Repeated accounts can warrant examining a broader practice.

Consider contrary evidence, privacy, and actual reporting responsibilities. A supportive discussion should not delay an established duty.

Feedback across the employee life cycle
Recruitment, onboarding, supervision, development, and retention involve chances to ask questions and challenge an interpretation.

Notice whether employees can raise a concern without losing credibility or opportunity. Examine actual responses rather than assume the climate.

Rewriting a defensive response
Privately revise: “That is not what I meant, and I have always supported equity.” Name the action, one relevant question, and a feasible response.

Keep any disputed fact precise. Leave reassurance and agreement out of the request.

Receiving feedback with care and responsibility
Hear the specific concern and examine your part. Discomfort need not become deflection.

Clarify proportionately, correct what is supported, and respect the person’s choices.

Follow through and examine repeated routines while keeping uncertainty and actual responsibilities visible.

title: Accessible Communication for the Person and the Task
audience: All staff; useful for supervisors, trainers, and public communication roles.
outcomes: Choose communication options by asking about the person’s task and preferences, so the information you share is accessible to that person and useful for what they need to do.
Recognize that language and disability access needs can occur together.
Preserve essential choices and information when changing format or pace.
Examine who is excluded when one communication method becomes the default.
summary: Choose communication options by asking about the person’s task and preferences, so the information you share is accessible to that person and useful for what they need to do.
body:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Accessible Communication for the Person and the Task
Choosing communication methods that preserve information, choice, and the person’s participation in DSD services and work.
Intermediate self-directed learning

Receiving, responding, and using information
Ask three questions: Can the person receive the message, respond in a usable way, and use the information afterward?

Privately examine a practice instruction. Which of those questions does its format answer, and which remain open?

Plain language, Easy Read, and accessibility
Plain language makes expression and organization clear. Easy Read uses simple text with images intended to support meaning.

Accessibility also concerns whether the person can receive and use the format. None of these choices automatically proves that the message works.

Translation and a remaining format barrier
A service notice has been translated, but its dense layout and scanned text remain difficult for a person to use.

Examine both language and format. One improvement should not hide a different unresolved access need.

Practice: a translated notice with a barrier
A service notice is translated, but a person says its scanned text and dense layout are difficult to use. What response best addresses the actual communication need?
A. Hear the specific task difficulty and arrange an appropriate language and format response without changing the notice’s meaning.
B. Repeat that translation made the notice accessible to everyone.
C. Remove essential choices and consequences to make the page much shorter.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Changing expression without removing a choice
A shorter explanation must keep essential options, requirements, and consequences accurate.

Use clear wording and sequence. Do not make a service decision disappear because it is difficult to explain.

Document structure that supports the task
Use descriptive headings, real text, and clear labels so readers can locate and interpret information. Do not rely on color alone.

A scanned image or an unlabeled field may block a task even when the visible page looks orderly.

Images that explain rather than distract
Choose an image because it supports the intended meaning. An attractive photograph may suggest a different action or outcome.

Provide appropriate text alternatives and examine what the text and image communicate together.

Spoken and recorded information
A recording may need captions, a transcript, or another appropriate method. The useful arrangement depends on the person and the task.

A written version is not automatically a substitute for every language or communication need.

Onboarding information that can be used
A new employee receives dense instructions and a recording without usable access features. Asking them to try harder leaves the information problem untouched.

Provide an appropriate explanation and format through the relevant arrangements while keeping the employee’s responsibilities clear.

Practice: an inaccessible orientation
A new employee says a dense instruction sheet and recorded orientation are difficult to use. What response best supports onboarding?
A. Ask the employee to explain a diagnosis to peers so the team can decide what to provide.
B. Hear the task and access need, use the appropriate arrangement, and make essential instructions available.
C. Assume the employee cannot perform the role because the orientation was not usable.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

A person using a communication aid
Address the person directly and leave time for their response. Do not finish a message or transfer the conversation to a companion without clarification.

Ask what helps the actual exchange. A device or speech difference does not establish understanding or decision capacity.

Visual information and different ways to read
A person may need real text, larger text, audio, another accessible format, or a description of visual information.

Describe the relevant content rather than point to it. The person’s preference and the actual task help guide the arrangement.

Pace, sequence, and predictability
Smaller steps, a clear sequence, and a usable summary may help someone follow a complex explanation. Ask rather than assume.

Predictable information can support participation without changing your respect for the person or requiring disclosure to peers.

Community perspectives on usability
People using the information can identify what the writer missed. Different responses may reveal different needs.

Culture briefs can prepare questions about language and relationships, while individuals describe their own format and support preferences.

A picture that changes the invitation’s meaning
An information-session invitation says attendance is optional and does not submit a service request. Its picture suggests receiving a service card.

Reader feedback identifies a conflict. Revise the combination and keep the actual purpose clear.

Practice: a conflicting invitation image
An invitation says an information session does not submit a service request. A reader thinks its card photograph means a service will be received. What response best addresses that feedback?
A. Keep the picture because staff know the intended meaning.
B. Assume every reader misunderstood and remove all images from every document.
C. Examine the text-image conflict, revise the relevant combination, and review its meaning appropriately.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Receiving an access request
Hear the particular difficulty and the requested method. Do not substitute the format you already made for the person’s account.

Follow the appropriate communication, language, or workplace access process. A respectful acknowledgment is different from an approved arrangement.

When one format becomes the only route
A standard format can repeatedly keep some people from reaching the same information and choices. Distribution alone does not establish access.

Examine the task, failures, and available alternatives. The barrier may belong to the communication method rather than the person.

Evidence that the communication works
Examine what a person understood and could use for the task. A request for another format identifies a need, not a comprehension result.

Keep specific feedback, missing information, and later effects distinct. Do not add a test as a new condition for service.

Communication across the employee life cycle
Recruitment, onboarding, supervision, development, and retention depend on usable information and opportunities to respond.

Privately revise a practice instruction. Preserve its essential meaning, identify a possible alternative method, and state what remains unknown about its usefulness.

Communication that preserves participation
Keep meaning, choice, and an adult relationship intact. Ask about the person’s actual task and method.

Consider language and disability access together when relevant.

Examine the delivered information, the person’s response, and repeated barriers rather than assume that one format works for everyone.

title: Supporting Informed Choice and Person-Centered Planning
audience: All staff; particularly relevant to service, policy, and provider-support roles.
outcomes: Support informed choice by clarifying the decision a person faces and explaining realistic options and uncertainties, a core part of person-centered planning.
Keep the person’s direction distinct from family, staff, or organizational preferences.
Recognize how cultural meaning, communication, and available supports affect participation.
Identify a planning routine that narrows options before a person can consider them.
summary: Support informed choice by clarifying the decision a person faces and explaining realistic options and uncertainties, a core part of person-centered planning.
body:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Supporting Informed Choice and Person-Centered Planning
Explaining meaningful options and chosen support so the person’s own direction can shape planning in DSD services and work.
Intermediate self-directed learning

The choice behind the question
Interest, a request for information, a preference, and agreement to an arrangement are different responses.

Privately examine “Are you okay with the program?” What choice does the question leave unclear, and what would the person need to know?

A person-centered starting point
Begin with the person’s life, strengths, priorities, and chosen relationships. A service menu is useful information, but it is not the whole goal.

Explain how available support relates to what matters to the person without promising an unconfirmed arrangement.

A familiar option placed first
A planning form lists a familiar service first and asks about community goals last. Staff begin preparing that service before hearing the person’s priorities.

Hearing the goal first can change which options are worth examining and what support would make participation possible.

Practice: a service listed before the goal
A planning form lists a familiar service first. Staff begin preparing it before hearing the person’s community goal. What response best supports person-centered planning?
A. Hear the person’s goal, compare realistic possibilities and support, and make unconfirmed arrangements clear.
B. Continue with the first service because a standard form makes the choice fair.
C. Promise the person any preferred service to show that their goal comes first.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Meaningful options and honest uncertainty
Explain what each option involves, the relevant tradeoffs, and what remains unconfirmed. Use the person’s goal to identify which differences matter.

Do not turn a possibility into an approved service or an inquiry into a completed choice.

Plain language that preserves the decision
Use clear words and consistent names for the options. Keep essential conditions and consequences intact.

A shorter explanation can still mislead if it removes the distinction the person needs to choose.

Chosen help and the person’s direction
Support may help a person compare information, ask questions, or communicate a choice. Clarify what help they want.

Advice is different from authority. A companion’s presence does not automatically make them the decision-maker.

An agreeable response with another meaning
“That sounds fine” may acknowledge an offer kindly while the person is still considering it. It may also express a choice.

Ask a clear question about the actual next step. Do not assign agreement from tone or a presumed cultural pattern.

An employee’s development goals
A supervisor assumes an employee with a disability wants a less demanding path. The employee’s own goal has not been discussed.

Ask about the desired development and actual task. Consider relevant support rather than take over the preference.

Practice: a protected development path
A supervisor assumes an employee with a disability wants a less demanding development assignment. The employee’s goals have not been discussed. What is the best response?
A. Offer only the easier assignment because protection is always the most respectful support.
B. Discuss the employee’s goals, the actual assignment requirements, and relevant support through the proper arrangements.
C. Require the employee to prove independence without support before offering any development.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Relationships and meanings of care
Some people want a trusted person involved; others prefer a private comparison. Both can reflect care and responsibility.

The person identifies the involvement they want. Do not make a family or community preference universal.

Information the person can use
Ask which difference matters and what information is still needed. Provide an appropriate method for receiving and responding.

A check should examine the explanation and task, rather than become an extra test before the person’s preference is considered.

Risk, preference, and realistic support
A preference may involve uncertainty or a tradeoff. Explain relevant information and support without using concern to decide for the person.

An unsupported promise is not choice, and an automatic protective refusal is not a complete assessment.

Community experience and planning quality
People with disabilities and families can help examine whether planning explanations support actual choice. Different experiences may identify different gaps.

Culture briefs prepare inquiry; the person’s priorities and chosen relationships remain specific.

A support offer that becomes a decision
A person asks a trusted supporter to help compare options. The supporter chooses one and communicates agreement before the person has decided.

Clarify the requested help and the actual preference. A helpful intention does not enlarge the supporter’s role.

Practice: comparison help becomes agreement
A person asks a trusted supporter to help compare options. The supporter selects one and communicates agreement before the person has chosen. What response best restores the distinction?
A. Accept the supporter’s choice because the relationship shows they know what is best.
B. Remove all help so the person must decide alone.
C. Clarify the requested assistance and the person’s actual preference, while checking any relevant authority.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Defaults that narrow participation
A default option, incomplete explanation, or presumed incapacity can repeatedly limit whose preferences shape a plan.

Examine offered options, usable information, chosen support, and recorded choices before concluding why outcomes differ.

The choice and its actual next effect
Describe whether the person wants information, further exploration, a confirmed option, or another response. Keep approval and authorization separate where required.

A recorded preference should not be expanded into a commitment the person did not make.

Evidence about meaningful participation
Examine what information was offered, what the person understood, how their preference shaped the next step, and what remained open.

Agreement, attendance, or a completed form alone cannot explain the quality of the choice.

Choice throughout the employee life cycle
Recruitment, onboarding, supervision, development, and retention involve preferences about goals and support, alongside actual work expectations.

Privately revise a practice planning question so it identifies the choice, available help, and next effect without taking over the answer.

A person’s direction with accurate support
Clarify the choice, realistic options, and uncertainty. Make information and participation usable.

Keep chosen assistance connected to the person’s preference and actual authority.

Examine repeated defaults that may narrow whose goals shape planning.

title: Making Meetings and Learning Materials Usable
audience: All staff who organize meetings or learning; useful for supervisors.
outcomes: Plan access across every stage of a meeting or learning session, from invitations and materials to participation and follow-up, so everyone can take part fully.
Check whether captions, visuals, and document structure preserve important meaning.
Respond to an access failure without placing the whole burden on the excluded person.
Compare attendance with the ability to understand and influence the discussion.
summary: Plan access across every stage of a meeting or learning session, from invitations and materials to participation and follow-up, so everyone can take part fully.
body:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Making Meetings and Learning Materials Usable
Planning access to the information, discussion, activities, and follow-up that make DSD meetings and learning meaningful.
Intermediate self-directed learning

The task people need to take part in
Identify what participants need to receive, understand, compare, and contribute. That purpose helps locate an access barrier.

Privately consider a meeting that compares two options. What information and response method would make the comparison possible?

The whole participation experience
Invitations, routes, materials, presentation, activities, and follow-up work together. One usable part cannot make every other part accessible.

Consider the in-person, virtual, or hybrid experience the actual task requires.

Captions and an inaccessible poll
A public service meeting has captions, but a participant cannot use the poll where options are compared.

An appropriate response route can preserve their choice and reason. Captions alone do not establish that the person could shape the recommendation.

Practice: captions but no usable response
A public service meeting has captions. A participant cannot use the poll that determines the option comparison. What response best preserves meaningful participation?
A. Provide a suitable way to submit the same choice and reason, with a chance to correct its restatement.
B. Treat captions and attendance as proof that the participant had full access.
C. Ask the participant to observe quietly while everyone else completes the poll.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Before the invitation is sent
Explain the purpose and how to ask about participation needs. Provide relevant materials through appropriate accessible arrangements.

Plan ordinary access needs early without assuming that a person’s identity predicts an individual method.

The route, room, and environment
Consider reaching the relevant place, receiving sound and visual information, and taking part comfortably enough for the task.

Room access differs from useful participation. Seating, light, sound, and a suitable alternative can matter in different ways.

Platforms and controls people can use
Participants may need to navigate without a mouse, find labeled controls, use captions, or receive shared content directly.

Examine the actual actions required to join, contribute, and use follow-up. A working link does not settle those questions.

Speech, captions, and important visuals
Check that captions preserve the spoken meaning and relevant sound. Make essential visual information available through an appropriate explanation.

A missing word such as “not” can reverse an instruction. The presence of captions alone does not establish accuracy.

Attendance without usable materials
An employee attends a work meeting but receives only an image of the material needed to compare a process.

A structured usable copy and appropriate response route can preserve their contribution. Attendance does not prove that they could participate.

Practice: a meeting page only shown as an image
An employee attends a process meeting but cannot use the image-only draft required for comparison. What response best preserves their contribution?
A. Record the employee as unprepared because they did not complete the comparison.
B. Provide a usable structured draft and an appropriate route for their reasoning through the actual arrangements.
C. Require the employee to ask a colleague to decide which option they would choose.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Time and more than one way to contribute
A clear question, room to consider it, and an appropriate written or spoken route can support different contributions.

Do not put everyone on the spot to prove participation. Preserve choice and the actual decision’s needs.

Materials that preserve meaning
Use clear structure, descriptive labels, and information participants can refer to during the actual activity.

Changing format should retain relevant options and uncertainty. Simplification should not remove the issue people are being asked to examine.

Help offered with a choice
Ask whether help would be useful and what the person wants it to accomplish. Do not rearrange or represent their contribution without clarification.

A chosen method can preserve authorship and participation while appropriate support is provided.

Community experience and prepared questions
People can help examine the full meeting experience, including the invitation and follow-up. Their needs and preferences may differ.

Culture briefs can support relevant preparation, but participants describe their own access and contribution choices.

Follow-up that keeps contributions available
A participant could not use the meeting activity but wants their reasoning considered before the recommendation is complete.

Clarify what remains open and provide a usable way to receive that contribution. A recording alone may not restore influence.

Practice: a recording after missed participation
A community participant missed an inaccessible response activity. The recommendation is still being developed. Staff plan only to send a recording. What would best address the lost contribution?
A. Treat viewing the recording as equivalent to influencing the comparison.
B. Tell the participant to wait for a future event without examining what remains open.
C. Explain what is still open and offer a usable way for their reason to enter the actual comparison.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

When access fails during the meeting
Name the task barrier without blaming the person. Consider a pause, a suitable alternative, or appropriate help based on the actual situation.

Avoid silently carrying on and later treating missing input as agreement. Explain any limit and how the concern will be addressed.

The repeated effect on knowledge and opportunity
Routine material and activity choices influence whose knowledge enters decisions and whose learning becomes visible.

Repeated exclusion can affect service recommendations and employee development. Examine the pathway rather than rely on attendance alone.

Evidence about what changed
Examine whether participants could use information, offer reasoning, correct a restatement, and influence what was genuinely open.

A sent agenda, attendance count, or caption icon can show an activity or feature without proving the whole experience worked.

A participation route across the employee life cycle
Recruitment, onboarding, supervision, development, and retention all include meetings and learning that shape opportunity.

Privately revise a practice comparison activity. Name the essential information, a usable response route, and what would show the contribution was considered.

Meetings and learning with usable participation
Plan the invitation, information, activity, and follow-up around the actual task. Preserve meaning and choice.

Respond to access failures through the appropriate arrangements.

Examine whose knowledge enters the work and what the evidence establishes about the change.

title: Neuroinclusive Work and Individualized Support
audience: All staff; supervisor focus for work design, feedback, and support.
outcomes: Telling an essential result apart from the familiar way of achieving it opens room for neuroinclusive work and individualized support. This course shows you how to make that distinction.
Make priorities, instructions, changes, and feedback understandable.
Respect privacy and use established accommodation responsibilities when needed.
Examine whether support continues across changes in role, supervision, or work setting.
summary: Telling an essential result apart from the familiar way of achieving it opens room for neuroinclusive work and individualized support. This course shows you how to make that distinction.
body:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Neuroinclusive Work and Individualized Support
Examine how instructions, work methods, and support continuity affect access and opportunity.
Intermediate self-directed learning

When the instruction is the obstacle
Think of a time when you knew the subject but could not tell which request mattered most.

In a practice service conversation, several instructions arrive together. Before judging the person's response, examine the sequence, the actual requirement, and what remains unclear.

Neurodiversity and individual needs
Neurodiversity describes variation in how people think and process information. It does not describe one shared set of strengths or needs.

Ask about the task and useful support. Eye contact, response speed, or a preference for writing cannot establish someone's diagnosis or ability.

A clearer sequence, the same requirement
A person receives three overlapping instructions about a service request. They miss the last step and are described as not following directions.

Explain one step at a time, retain important conditions, and check what the person understands. Repeated unclear instructions could otherwise turn a design problem into a record about the person.

Several instructions and a missed service step
A person misses the last of three overlapping instructions. The requirement still applies. Which response best examines the barrier?
A. Clarify the sequence, offer useful support, and check understanding.
B. Record that the person cannot manage the process independently.
C. Remove the requirement without checking the applicable process.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

An essential result and a familiar method
An accurate explanation of a policy is a work result. Giving it without notes in a rapid exchange may be a familiar method.

Ask which parts are necessary for the purpose and which can vary. A different method must still allow the required knowledge, accuracy, and judgment to be demonstrated.

Priorities that can be understood
'Handle this soon' leaves the timing, depth, and priority uncertain. Several such requests can create competing expectations.

Explain the result needed, relevant timing, and what has priority. When circumstances change, name the change instead of assuming everyone has recognized a new order.

Information that remains available
A spoken instruction may disappear before someone has organized it. A written record can help, if it is clear and accessible.

Keep the necessary conditions and the next step together. More pages are not always more useful; compare whether the person can find and act on the important information.

Sensory and social conditions
Noise, interruption, lighting, and the pace of a conversation may affect participation. Different people experience those conditions differently.

Discuss workable conditions with the person. Do not assign a quieter role, less visible work, or reduced opportunity merely because you assume it would be comfortable.

Support when the work changes
An employee moves to a development assignment with a new supervisor. Written priorities that helped in the earlier role are no longer available.

Examine what the new task requires and what support needs to continue through the appropriate process. A transition should not become an unexamined test of working without support.

A development assignment changes supervisors
An employee's written priorities disappear in a new assignment. Their work becomes harder to organize. What should the supervisor examine first?
A. Whether the employee can succeed without any support.
B. The actual work conditions and support continuity through the proper route.
C. The employee's medical history in a team discussion.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Support and the proper route
Clearer work design can help broadly. An individual accommodation request also has a specific process and responsible people.

Stay within your role, respond respectfully, and use the appropriate route. Do not collect a diagnosis for a general conversation or promise an arrangement you cannot authorize.

Privacy and a useful handoff
A receiving supervisor may need to understand a work arrangement without receiving the person's whole personal history.

Use the appropriate process to carry necessary information forward. Ask what is needed for the task and who should receive it, rather than making the employee explain private matters to each new colleague.

Feedback about the work
'You are not leadership material' hides the evidence and the expected result. 'The comparison omitted the service limit' identifies something that can be examined.

Discuss the work, its conditions, and the improvement needed. Separate a missed requirement from a judgment based on style, pace, or a preferred way of communicating.

Community experience expands the question
People with different disability experiences may describe different barriers in the same service. No single account can represent everyone.

Use community knowledge to examine the route and improve questions. Culture briefs provide background; they cannot predict an individual's processing style, preferences, or support needs.

Listening without prescribing a method
A participant asks for questions in advance but wants to contribute during the meeting as well. Staff assume written comments should replace attendance.

Offer preparation without removing the person's preferred participation. Repeatedly assigning people to a separate route may reduce their influence even when the intention is supportive.

Preparation without exclusion
A participant requests advance questions and also wants to attend the discussion. Which response best preserves participation?
A. Send questions but remove the person from the meeting.
B. Assume everyone with a similar identity wants this arrangement.
C. Provide the requested preparation and discuss a usable way to participate.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

The accumulated effect on opportunity
Unclear instructions, lost support, and style-based feedback can reinforce one another across assignments.

Trace the sequence: what condition made the task difficult, how the response was interpreted, and what opportunity followed. A plausible mechanism still needs evidence before it becomes a finding about inequity.

Evidence before a conclusion
Compare the task, the available support, the person's account, and the result. Note what is missing.

Do not infer ability from one response or fairness from the absence of a complaint. Look for repeated conditions and differences in the route while protecting personal information.

Rewrite a method-based judgment
Consider this practice feedback: 'They need written priorities, so they are not ready for complex work.'

Rewrite it around the actual task, available support, and evidence. Ask what remains unknown and whether the method being judged is essential to the work.

Support across the employee life cycle
Access can change during recruitment, onboarding, assignments, development, advancement, and transitions. A useful arrangement at one stage may be lost at another.

Consider a practice transition. What result must stay intact, what method could vary, and what appropriate support route would help preserve access without unnecessary disclosure?

Meaningful access with individual support
Keep the work result clear, examine the conditions, and listen to the person's expressed needs.

Use appropriate support processes and protect privacy. When a routine repeatedly narrows participation or opportunity, investigate the mechanism and the evidence rather than assuming the person lacks capability.

title: Using Culture Briefs to Prepare, Listen, and Learn
audience: All staff; useful for supervisors and people preparing community conversations.
outcomes: Use a culture brief’s history, institutions and perspectives to develop thoughtful questions, so you can prepare well, listen closely and keep learning from the people you meet.
Distinguish a contextual generalization from a claim about an individual.
Seek varied perspectives without expecting one partner to represent a whole community.
Revise an invitation or explanation in light of what people actually say.
summary: Use a culture brief’s history, institutions and perspectives to develop thoughtful questions, so you can prepare well, listen closely and keep learning from the people you meet.
body:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Using Culture Briefs to Prepare, Listen, and Learn
Use community knowledge to prepare thoughtful questions while leaving individual answers with the person.
Intermediate self-directed learning

A useful fact or an assumed answer
Consider the difference between 'Family may matter in this conversation' and 'This person wants relatives involved.'

The first can prompt preparation. The second makes a decision without the person's answer. Think about a familiar assumption you could turn into an open question.

A brief is situated knowledge
A community brief draws together information from particular sources, places, and dates. It is a starting point for learning.

Check its scope and limits. Differences within a community, changing conditions, and the person's own account may matter more than the broad pattern you first notice.

From a family pattern to a chosen invitation
A team reads that some families discuss important decisions together. It plans to invite relatives to every service conversation.

Ask who each person wants involved and what support would help. Repeated automatic invitations could expose private information or shift influence away from the person whose service is being discussed.

Family participation in a service conversation
A brief mentions shared family decisions. Staff plan to invite relatives before asking the person. Which response uses the brief well?
A. Ask who the person wants involved and what support would help.
B. Invite relatives because the pattern is well documented.
C. Avoid any question about chosen support to prevent stereotyping.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Read the source before using the number
A population estimate needs its date, location, category, and source. A number in a brief may not describe the people using a particular service.

Check the original source and what it measured before using the estimate in a decision. Missing or unfinished material is an open question, not a program fact.

Generalizations that remain open
A generalization describes a pattern with limits. A stereotype assigns a fixed expectation to a person because of apparent membership.

Ask whether contrary evidence can change your account. Even a flattering assumption can restrict opportunity if it assigns someone a role they did not choose.

Access questions with individual answers
Ask about preferred language, communication, format, and chosen support as relevant to the task. Do not fill in the answers from a name or appearance.

A brief can help you prepare available options. The person's expressed needs and the actual service requirements guide the encounter.

Curiosity without unnecessary disclosure
A brief may mention migration, religion, or historical harm. Those topics are not an invitation to request a person's private history.

Ask what the task genuinely requires through the proper process. You can show interest and respect without asking someone to explain trauma or prove that a community description fits.

A colleague's role is not in a brief
A supervisor reads a brief before welcoming a colleague, then asks the employee to explain their community at the next meeting.

Invite the colleague's own interests and learning goals instead. Repeated identity-based requests may add unpaid explanatory work and displace assignments that support the employee's chosen development.

A welcome that assigns extra work
A supervisor asks a new colleague to teach the team about their community. The colleague has expressed interest in policy research. What is the better response?
A. Treat identity as evidence of expertise and continue the request.
B. Ask about the colleague's own expertise and chosen development interests.
C. Never discuss community learning anywhere in the team.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Community partners and agreed roles
A community partner can offer situated expertise. An interpreter, cultural broker, advocate, and organization may have different responsibilities.

Explain the decision and the contribution being requested. Do not assume a partner speaks for everyone or can supply private information about individuals.

Preparation that leads to a real question
Before outreach, identify what staff need to learn and what remains open. Use the brief to improve that question.

Ask how the actual message and response route work for people. Questions about trust or welcome should invite experience, not prescribe a community's preferred answer.

Who is reached and who can respond
A familiar organization may help reach people, but its members are not the whole community. The response method can also narrow participation.

Examine invitations, language, access, timing, and the decision still open. Attendance alone cannot show that the range of relevant experience influenced the work.

Changing an account after listening
A participant says the brief's description does not fit their experience. Receive the correction and ask what matters in this decision.

Separate the person's account from broader claims that need further review. Learning improves when contrary evidence can change the explanation rather than being dismissed as an exception.

An invitation grounded in the person's choice
Outreach staff assume a trusted organization should receive all later updates on a person's behalf. The person has asked for direct information.

Discuss the requested contact and any chosen support. A relationship that helped with outreach does not automatically authorize someone else to receive or decide personal service information.

A partner and a later contact preference
A partner helped a person find a service. The person now requests direct updates, but staff prefer to send everything through the partner. What should happen?
A. Assume the earlier help authorizes every later contact.
B. Use the brief to decide whom the person should trust.
C. Clarify the person's requested contact and any chosen support through the actual process.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

When assumptions become routine criteria
An unsupported cultural explanation can move from a conversation into a record, a targeting rule, or an assignment pattern.

Trace the action and its possible effect. Repeated use may sustain unequal treatment, but findings require evidence about actual criteria and consequences, not identity-based suspicion.

Evidence that keeps the inquiry honest
Separate what the brief says, what the person described, what staff did, and what followed. Note the missing links.

Look for changes in access or influence after a revised practice. A respectful conversation matters, but it does not establish that every service or workplace barrier has been removed.

Rewrite a cultural shortcut
Privately revise this practice statement: 'People from this community want family involved, so we include relatives by default.'

Keep the useful preparation but remove the assumed answer. Include an open question, the actual boundary, and what you still need to learn from the person.

Learning across service and workplace stages
Briefs can support outreach, onboarding, supervision, and shared learning. At every stage, keep people's own choices and expertise visible.

Review whether knowledge opens a question or assigns a role. The useful result is better understanding and more appropriate practice, with honest limits on what the evidence establishes.

Prepare thoughtfully, let people answer
Use a brief to widen inquiry, check its evidence, and prepare usable options. Listen to the person's own account.

When a cultural assumption becomes a repeated decision rule, examine its effects and revise the route. A brief is most useful when it supports respectful learning rather than replacing it.

title: Language Access Across a Whole Service Encounter
audience: All staff; useful for supervisors, public communication, and service roles.
outcomes: Learn to prepare a conversation with qualified language support in place, so that throughout the encounter you speak directly to the person rather than to the interpreter.
Write source text that preserves conditions and decisions through translation.
Trace language access from invitation through the response and follow-up.
Recognize when reliance on family or bilingual coworkers shifts an inappropriate burden.
summary: Learn to prepare a conversation with qualified language support in place, so that throughout the encounter you speak directly to the person rather than to the interpreter.
body:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Language Access Across a Whole Service Encounter
Trace the language route from first information to a usable response, with accurate meaning and appropriate support.
Intermediate self-directed learning

Where the conversation stops
Imagine understanding a notice but reaching a response line you cannot use. The message has arrived; the task remains unfinished.

Trace what the person must do next. A successful translation does not establish that the response, clarification, or later update is usable.

Translation and interpretation are different
Translation conveys written meaning across languages. Interpretation supports communication in spoken or signed exchanges.

Both require appropriate competence and a clear purpose. A person's conversational English, a colleague's bilingual ability, or an automated draft does not by itself establish fitness for a consequential service task.

A translated notice and a closed response route
A practice notice explains a service question in the person's preferred language, but its only response line operates in English.

Clarify an appropriate assistance route and explain it accurately. Repeated gaps at that step could affect whose questions are heard and whose requests continue; the cause needs actual evidence.

The next step after a translated notice
A translated notice leads to an English-only response line. The person cannot ask a follow-up question. What is the most useful response?
A. Examine and explain the appropriate language-supported response route.
B. Record that the notice was sent and the person chose not to reply.
C. Translate more background pages without checking the response step.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Preserve the conditions in source text
Before translation, make the action, relevant conditions, dates, and responsibilities explicit. Avoid unexplained acronyms and expressions.

A shorter sentence must not change eligibility, choice, or a required next step. Clear source text gives language professionals a better basis for conveying the intended meaning.

Review what the final message means
Qualified review and questions about actual meaning matter. A translated title or a polished layout cannot establish accuracy.

Examine the complete message and the response route. If a condition changes, the related versions need appropriate attention; an earlier translation may no longer convey the current explanation.

Speak with the person
When an interpreter supports an encounter, address the person directly and allow time for meaning to be conveyed.

Use clear sections and explain unfamiliar terms. The staff member remains responsible for the service information; the interpreter's role does not transfer the substantive decision or explanation.

Time for questions and clarification
Language-supported conversations need room for the person's questions, not only staff instructions.

Check the meaning of the next step respectfully. A nod or a brief answer does not establish understanding of complex conditions, and a request for clarification is not evidence of poor cooperation.

A bilingual employee's assigned work
A colleague is repeatedly pulled from development work to interpret unrelated discussions. Their language knowledge is treated as an unlimited resource.

Use appropriate qualified arrangements and examine role, workload, and opportunity. Helpful personal knowledge does not automatically create an interpreter assignment or replace the required process.

Language knowledge and development time
A bilingual colleague is repeatedly asked to interpret unrelated meetings, displacing a policy assignment. Which response best addresses the situation?
A. Continue because the colleague has never complained.
B. Use proper qualified arrangements and examine the colleague's role and displaced work.
C. Exclude the colleague from all language-related work.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

An assistance route people can find
Explain how appropriate language assistance can be requested and what the actual route provides. Availability that is difficult to discover may not help.

Check the notice, contact method, and later response together. Do not promise a particular arrangement, timing, or cost treatment unless the applicable process establishes it.

CLAS and the supporting organization
CLAS connects respectful communication with leadership, workforce support, community engagement, and improvement in health and health care.

Use it as a framework for examining the whole experience. It does not certify a service as compliant or establish an individual's outcome because one document is translated.

Language and disability access together
A preferred language does not settle format, hearing, vision, literacy, or other communication needs. More than one consideration may shape the same task.

Ask about useful support and examine the actual material. Avoid assuming that translation alone resolves every barrier or that one format works for everyone.

Community input on actual material
Community experience can reveal an unclear expression, an unavailable response route, or a meaning staff missed.

Ask about the specific message and task. A partner's account does not speak for every language user, and community feedback does not replace appropriate qualified language review.

A revision that keeps all steps connected
Participants understand the translated notice but cannot find how to ask a follow-up question. Staff propose adding more translated background pages.

Examine the missing response step first. Additional information may be useful, but it cannot substitute for a usable route to clarification.

More pages or a usable question route
Community participants understand a notice but cannot find how to ask a question. Staff propose adding several translated background pages. What should be examined?
A. Whether participants can memorize the existing notice.
B. Whether the community brief predicts their preferred communication.
C. The missing response step and the actual assistance arrangement.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

From one gap to a recurring barrier
An English-only next step can undo language access at the beginning. Repeated reliance on one bilingual employee can narrow that employee's opportunity.

Trace the specific action and possible effect. Examine encounters, responsibilities, and missing evidence before attributing a difference to language, culture, or discrimination.

What the evidence can establish
Delivery, translation, understanding, response, and service outcome are different events. Record only what the available evidence supports.

Listen to accounts of the route and compare actual steps. An unanswered message cannot establish disinterest, and a satisfied reader cannot establish that every later service question is resolved.

Rewrite the missing next step
Privately revise this practice instruction: 'Respond using the contact number below.' The notice is translated, but the line offers no stated language route.

Explain the actual assistance route or name what must be confirmed before use. Retain the service conditions, and do not invent a promise about unavailable support.

Support across the employee life cycle
Recruitment, onboarding, assignments, development, and transitions need clear language responsibilities and usable resources.

Recognize language expertise without assuming unlimited extra work. Examine whether recurring assistance demands affect workload, credit, and access to development, and use appropriate guidance for role questions.

Follow the whole language route
Preserve meaning, use appropriate language assistance, and examine how people ask and answer questions throughout the encounter.

Learn from actual material and experience. Trace recurring gaps and workload effects with evidence, while keeping individual preferences, authority, and uncertainty clear.

title: Community Engagement With an Honest Account of Influence
audience: All staff; useful for supervisors and people planning engagement.
outcomes: Before inviting people to participate, you will learn to be clear about what they can actually shape, so their involvement rests on an honest account of their influence.
Compare ways to include people whose experience is missing.
Recognize participation costs, access needs, and the value of community expertise.
Explain how input affected the choice and what could not change.
summary: Before inviting people to participate, you will learn to be clear about what they can actually shape, so their involvement rests on an honest account of their influence.
body:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Community Engagement With an Honest Account of Influence
Examine what people can shape, what participation requires, and how their input reaches an actual decision.
Intermediate self-directed learning

An invitation before or after the choice
Imagine being asked to help shape an onboarding guide after its content has already been settled. What can your contribution still change?

An honest invitation names the remaining question. A useful review can occur after a decision, but it should not be described as shared design of a choice that is closed.

Different depths of participation
Informing explains. Seeking input asks for a response. Shared design involves people in shaping alternatives. Shared decision-making includes actual authority.

Each can be useful when named accurately. Attendance, an advisory title, or a distribution list does not establish the depth of the relationship.

Two communication designs still open
In this example, a service team compares two ways to explain a response process. Both designs can still change.

Invite people to examine complete alternatives and explain the choice they can influence. Repeatedly asking only after decisions are fixed may preserve existing power while creating the appearance of shared design.

Comparing two service explanations
Two practice service explanations remain open. Which invitation best supports meaningful input?
A. Explain the alternatives, constraints, and what participant input can change.
B. Ask participants to endorse the version staff prefer.
C. Describe a shared decision even though staff retain the actual authority.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Who is affected and who is invited
A familiar partner list may not include the range of people affected. Some invited participants may still be unable to use the response route.

Examine the relationship between the decision and the experience sought. Do not ask one person to stand for everyone who shares an identity or service connection.

Preparation that makes choices understandable
Participants need enough clear information to examine the question. Explain the purpose, alternatives, constraints, and intended use of input.

Use appropriate language and accessible formats. A large background packet cannot substitute for a clear account of what people are being asked to consider.

Participation has costs
Time, travel, communication support, preparation, and other conditions can affect who participates. Some burdens are less visible inside an office.

Discuss feasible arrangements through the appropriate process. Do not promise payment or resources without authority, and do not assume willingness means participation has no cost.

The person's direction and chosen support
A family member may contribute important experience. The person using a service may want help, direct participation, or another arrangement.

Keep the person's purpose and chosen support visible. Family input should not automatically replace their own voice or be treated as evidence that everyone shares the same preference.

Staff input with a truthful promise
A team asks employees to help design onboarding after the new guide is fixed. Staff can still identify problems in use, but cannot choose its initial content.

Explain the real review opportunity or reopen a defined choice through the appropriate authority. Repeated overstated invitations can weaken trust and hide whose input shapes workplace practice.

Employee input after an onboarding decision
The onboarding guide is final, but staff are invited to help design it. Which response is most honest?
A. Keep the label because employees are attending.
B. Name a genuine review question, or establish an open choice through the proper authority.
C. Cancel all staff feedback because the first version is fixed.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Listening to experience and examining the task
An account can reveal a burden that staff overlooked. Ask how it connects to the specific choice, without requiring a private history.

Different accounts may point to different needs. Compare them with the actual process and relevant evidence rather than assuming one story supplies a complete answer.

A contribution that reaches the comparison
Show how input changes an option, identifies a concern, or supports a reason for keeping part of the design.

A thank-you alone does not explain influence. Some suggestions may not be adopted; describe the relevant reasons without implying that the contributor's experience was invalid.

Clear responsibilities without false authority
People need to know who can decide and what staff can realistically promise. Learning activities do not transfer agency authority.

Name the relevant boundary in ordinary language. Where a decision or resource is uncertain, seek appropriate guidance instead of describing a shared power that has not been established.

Report back with something people can examine
Return the relevant choice, reasons, and limits in a usable form. Explain what happened to the input and what remains open.

Protect private material and respect acknowledgment preferences. A complete report-back is about the defined task; it need not claim that all future questions are closed.

Acknowledgment is not universal agreement
One participant says the revised message reflects their concern. Another has not replied. Those are different facts.

Record the actual responses without treating silence as approval or one positive comment as a population outcome. The report-back may be complete while the use of the design remains untested.

A positive reply and a missing reply
One participant says the revised message reflects their concern. Another has not replied. How should the account describe the result?
A. Everyone supports the decision because nobody objected.
B. The service outcome improved for all participants.
C. One concern was recognized in the revision; other views and actual-use effects remain unknown.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

How recurring invitations distribute influence
Timing, information, access, and familiar networks can repeatedly determine who shapes alternatives and who only reacts afterward.

Trace the route from invitation to contribution to decision. Examine actual opportunities and consequences before making a finding about inequity.

Evidence of an honest relationship
Compare what was promised, what participants could use, how input was considered, and what was returned.

Distinguish reach, attendance, influence, and later effects. People can value a conversation while still identifying an unresolved service barrier or a limit on the decision.

Rewrite an overstated invitation
Privately revise this practice message: 'Help us design the new guide. The final version has already been approved.'

Name the actual opportunity and what can change. If no choice is open, describe information sharing or a later review honestly instead of promising shared design.

Engagement across learning and workplace stages
Community learning can deepen service practice. Employee input can improve onboarding, development, and transitions when its influence is clear.

Recognize expertise without assigning representative duties from identity. Use briefs to prepare questions and appropriate relationships to learn from varied experience.

Make the promise match the opportunity
Name what is open, support usable participation, and show how input reaches the actual decision.

Return an honest account with appropriate limits. When a repeated arrangement narrows influence, investigate the route and its effects rather than treating participation counts as the whole relationship.

title: Clear Public Information That People Can Use
audience: All staff preparing explanations; useful for supervisors reviewing public materials.
outcomes: Good public information starts from what the reader needs to know. This course shows how to organize an explanation around the reader’s question and the next step they need to take.
Preserve eligibility conditions, duties, and uncertainties while making them clearer.
Compare the meaning carried by text, images, and accessible formats.
Use feedback about understanding to revise the information rather than judging the reader.
summary: Good public information starts from what the reader needs to know. This course shows how to organize an explanation around the reader’s question and the next step they need to take.
body:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Clear Public Information That People Can Use
Make explanations usable without losing important conditions, choices, or the next step.
Intermediate self-directed learning

Accurate words, an unclear task
