Choose a subject and complete two thoughts: what the learner should understand, and what question they should be able to examine.

Connect a service and workplace example where useful. Keep personal reflection legitimate without requiring a report or a prescribed action from every learner.

Examine learning and work conditions separately
A reasoned practice response can show how a learner approaches the supplied case. Actual service use and workplace conditions require their own evidence.

Keep the inquiry useful and proportionate. Do not infer a private belief or assign an intercultural level from a course response.

Keep the resource connected to current work
Review subject accuracy, source changes, user questions, and practical fit through the responsibilities already in place.

A resource can remain valuable while needing revision. Do not let familiar wording become permanent when the relevant work or evidence has changed.

Learning that strengthens independent practice
Substantive explanation, relevant practice, usable access, and guidance can help staff deepen understanding and examine equity within their responsibilities.

The program extends support across the division while preserving shared learning choices, private reflection, and actual decision processes.

title: Putting Three ADSA Equity Goals into Practice
audience: Supervisors and managers developing their three-goal work plans with consultant guidance; staff examining how selected goals connect with service delivery, workplace opportunity, and actual responsibilities.
outcomes: Learn to explain the six ADSA goals in the program’s documented wording, so you can describe them accurately as you put equity goals into practice in your own work.
Select three relevant goals and connect each with a real organizational condition.
Examine how the three selected goals reinforce one another or create competing demands across service and workplace conditions, and use relevant evidence to guide follow-through.
Identify where consultation and guidance would help clarify the plan.
summary: Learn to explain the six ADSA goals in the program’s documented wording, so you can describe them accurately as you put equity goals into practice in your own work.
body:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Putting Three ADSA Equity Goals into Practice
Connect three relevant ADSA equity goals with the conditions, responsibilities, and evidence that can support meaningful action.
Advanced self-directed learning

Start with the shared understanding
In the One DSD arrangement, the Equity Director briefs leadership on the six ADSA goals and answers their questions.

Supervisors and managers then use the work plan to select three goals and put them into practice, with the consultant providing consultation and guidance as needed.

The six goals in the program
Eliminating disparities; Community engagement; Hiring and retention.

Learning and development; Contracts and procurement; Communication and accessibility.

Select three relevant to the work, with reasons. The choice does not imply that the other goals are unimportant or that every course must address all six.

Worked example: three connected goals
Practice question: people can read a service notice but cannot use the follow-up route.

Selected goals: Communication and accessibility; Community engagement; Contracts and procurement.

The plan examines the route, affected people’s accounts, and relevant provider expectations. Actual authority and a better result remain open.

Three goals attached to a notice
A practice area selects Communication and accessibility, Community engagement, and Contracts and procurement for a service notice with an unusable follow-up route. Which plan is most useful?
A. Examine the route, affected accounts, and provider expectations through actual roles; keep effects and unknowns visible.
B. Count three presentations and declare all three goals achieved.
C. Change a provider contract immediately because selecting the goal supplies authority.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Find the work before adding another process
An existing service review, learning arrangement, or workforce practice may already address part of the goal. Examine it before proposing a duplicate.

A missing work-plan row does not establish that equity work is absent. Identify what is actually done and where a supported gap remains.

Describe the condition and possible mechanism
State what people encounter and how a routine may repeatedly shape access, opportunity, or burden. Keep observations and explanations distinct.

A usable plan asks about a specific mechanism. It does not assume that every difference proves discrimination or that one activity eliminates disparities.

Ask why these three belong together
Explain what each selected goal contributes to the question and where their actions may reinforce or complicate one another.

Do not assume that more activity means more progress. A change supporting one goal may create a burden relevant to another.

Community knowledge before choices close
Invite relevant perspectives to examine the condition and alternatives while the decision can still be informed. Explain the available influence and actual limits.

A contribution does not imply endorsement or representation of a whole community. Use the account to improve the question, not decorate a finished plan.

Compare feasible responses
Compare the current approach and practical alternatives for relevant access, benefit, burden, resources, and actual requirements.

Seek consultant analysis and guidance where helpful. A proposal should name its uncertainty rather than claim an effect that has not been examined.

A workforce plan built around the same circle
A practice area selects Hiring and retention, Learning and development, and Eliminating disparities. Only staff already familiar with the manager receive preparation for development assignments. What should the plan examine?
A. The manager’s friends as proof of misconduct.
B. A universal requirement that everyone accept the same assignment.
C. Examine information, preparation, support, and task criteria across the route, preserving actual processes and staff choice.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Workforce goals across the life cycle
A practice area connects Hiring and retention, Learning and development, and Eliminating disparities around access to useful preparation and assignments.

Examine recruitment, onboarding, support, development, recognition, and transition where relevant. The same condition can carry forward, but the full effect needs evidence.

Learning and guidance extend capability
Resources can support substantive understanding, private reflection, and practice in the actual subject. Staff can use them voluntarily and seek guidance when useful.

Learning is part of the plan where it fits the goal. It should not replace examination of a service rule, opportunity route, or other condition that requires action.

Culture briefs support the inquiry
Use briefs to prepare questions about meaning, communication, and participation. Ask people what matters in the particular service or workplace situation.

A brief cannot select the three goals for a community or predict an individual’s preference. Keep the actual account and the plan’s question central.

Make responsibility understandable
Describe the proposed action and the actual role that can consider or carry it out. Do not assign new authority, workloads, or partner duties from a template.

Where a dependency remains, name the question plainly. Required policy, employment, service, and other processes continue through their responsible roles.

Separate action from intended result
A revised notice, reviewed requirement, or supported learning opportunity is an action or output. Usable clarification or opportunity is an intended result to examine.

Choose evidence that fits the question. Missing experience remains unknown, and an appealing proposal is not a completed outcome.

Claimed agreement in the work-plan update
A participant suggests a clearer question route. The proposed route has not been used. A practice progress update says the community agreed with the plan and disparities were eliminated. What account is supported?
A. The original update because the suggestion was useful.
B. The account informed a proposed route; actual use, wider agreement, and effects remain unexamined through the appropriate review.
C. No progress can be described until every long-term result is known.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

A progress account that helps the work
Describe what is prepared, examined, carried out, and still open. Keep the selected goals and relevant evidence connected with the actual question.

The account can fit an existing work plan. This course does not prescribe a timetable, reporting cycle, or a new administrative structure.

Draft the three-goal connection
Choose a practice or actual question and explain why three goals fit. For each, name the condition, possible action, and evidence question.

Which part requires consultant guidance or another actual responsibility? Keep the proposed plan separate from approval and do not prescribe a date that has not been agreed.

Respond to an unresolved condition
If a proposed change cannot yet proceed, explain the reason and the relevant next question. Do not hide the gap or invent a decision power to close it.

Consultation can help examine alternatives and recommendations. An actual accommodation, complaint, safety issue, or required review still follows its own process.

Examine actual use and revise thoughtfully
After an action occurs, compare its use and remaining conditions with the original question. Explain changes in scope or context.

Different evidence may support different findings. A narrower gain can be meaningful while broader disparities, trust, or lasting effects remain unestablished.

Three goals, one meaningful work connection
Select three goals with reasons, examine the actual condition and alternatives, and connect action with evidence and appropriate responsibilities.

The consultant provides guidance as needed. The plan supports useful equity practice without replacing shared understanding, existing processes, or the people who carry out the work.

title: Policy and Legislative Analysis through an Equity Lens
audience: DSD staff and leaders whose work involves policy, legislative proposals, service design, fiscal analysis, community engagement, or implementation; relevant to the contributions of the Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant and colleagues across DHS.
outcomes: Distinguish policy, legislative, bill, and fiscal analysis and explain their contributions to a recommendation.
Read an actual Minnesota provision and distinguish its requirements from implementation and observed results.
Use community knowledge, staff experience, and evidence to identify barriers and compare alternatives.
Explain resource needs and the distribution of benefits and burdens without treating an estimate as an outcome.
Write and revise a concise recommendation whose equity reasoning is visible in the work itself.
summary: Using real Minnesota policy and legislative records, you will weigh community and staff perspectives and practice writing recommendations with equity embedded throughout.
body:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Policy and Legislative Analysis through an Equity Lens
Understand the policy question, examine proposed changes to law, and develop recommendations that make equity part of the work.
Advanced self-directed learning

What are we analyzing?
A policy guides decisions and action.
Policy analysis examines a problem, compares responses, and assesses consequences.
Legislative analysis examines proposed changes to law.
Bill analysis identifies what specific provisions and amendments would change.

What you will learn and practice
Read a provision and explain its practical meaning.
Weigh community experience alongside staff knowledge and other evidence.
Compare benefits, burdens, and resource needs.
Write a recommendation and revise it when the evidence or text changes.

Waiver Reimagine provides a real case
The 2026 law adds advance budget and service information and a phased transition to the two-waiver structure.
DHS’s July 2026 update explains that a new launch date had not been determined.
Read the legal change and the dated implementation account together.

From legal language to people’s choices
Read the requirement
Understand the intended benefit
Examine people’s experience
Compare ways to carry it out
Recommend support and follow-through

Practice reading the Waiver Reimagine change
The law adds advance planning information and phased implementation. The July 2026 DHS update says no new launch date has been set. Which conclusion is supported?
A. The requirement has changed; examine how people will receive and use the information during transition.
B. The new waiver arrangements are already operating for everyone because the Legislature acted.
C. The legal change is still only a suggestion because the launch date has not been set.
Choose a response to explore the reasoning.

Equity changes the substance of the analysis
Ask whose experience defines the problem, whose knowledge informs the evidence, and how each option distributes benefits and burdens.
Use the DHS Equity Analysis Toolkit to deepen those questions throughout the work and explain how they affect the recommendation.

Trace the effect you expect to see
Start with a specific feature of the proposal. Explain what it asks people or staff to do and why that could change access, opportunity, or choice.
Consider disability, race, language, geography, and other conditions where they help explain the issue.

Use culture briefs to ask better questions
A culture brief can prepare you to ask about trust, communication, participation, and experience with services.
It cannot predict an individual’s priorities. Check assumptions with people affected by the work and preserve differences within a community.

Whose knowledge influences the recommendation?
Bring legislative, program, fiscal, equity, and service experience into the discussion. Make room for staff who implement decisions as well as those who approve them.
Ask how contributions changed the recommendation, not only who attended.

A second public example brings community evidence
DHS’s intervention and respite service redesign connects a legislatively directed study with service proposals and feedback.
Its 2026 survey summary raises concerns about overlapping services and provider responsibilities.
Use that concern to ask what a revised service design should clarify.

Read the survey as evidence, not a verdict
Respondents’ expectations about culturally specific needs
28: goal met or likely met
17: unsure
7: goal not met or unlikely
52 responses to this item

Keep the denominator with the finding
Response | Count | Item total | Share
Met / likely met | 28 | 52 | 53.8%
Unsure | 17 | 52 | 32.7%
Not met / unlikely | 7 | 52 | 13.5%

Practice using community feedback
A draft recommendation cites the chart as evidence that the design meets every community’s needs. The survey report also identifies limited direct input from people using services. Which revision is strongest?
A. Keep the conclusion because the positive category contains more responses than either other category.
B. Describe the responses and limits, investigate concerns, and seek missing perspectives before settling the design.
C. Remove all community evidence because this survey cannot establish what every person needs.
Choose a response to explore the reasoning.

Fiscal analysis and equity analysis inform each other
A fiscal note estimates the financial effects of a bill. It does not decide the bill’s merits.
Equity analysis also examines how benefits, costs, and effort are distributed. Ask who pays, who does the work, and whose burden an estimate may miss.

Make resource assumptions meaningful
For each option, ask what people must understand or do, who will support them, and what time and expertise that requires.
Separate a known cost from an estimate. Explain what could change the estimate and whether an apparent saving shifts work to someone else.

Engagement should be able to change the answer
Identify the decision people can influence. Ask whose experience is missing and what may prevent participation.
Use their contribution to revise the comparison of options. Explain afterward what changed, what did not, and why.

Compare options against the same purpose
Use a clear purpose, such as helping people understand support choices during a transition.
Compare likely benefit, remaining barriers, staff and partner work, and evidence needed.
A recommendation should explain the tradeoff rather than hide it.

Compare ways to support informed choices
Approach | Potential benefit | Remaining question | Staff or partner work | Evidence needed
General guidance | Shared explanation | Individual questions? | Keep guidance clear | Can people use it?
Guidance and discussion | Tailored understanding | Who can participate? | Prepare staff to explain | Which questions persist?
Co-review and discussion | Improve relevance | Whose input is missing? | Hear and respond to input | What changed and helped?

Changes in the text can change the advice
Compare the 2025 and 2026 Waiver Reimagine provisions. The later law replaces a fixed date in paragraph (g) with advance information tied to when a person’s services become subject to the budget, and adds phased implementation.
Revisit any conclusion that depends on the earlier wording.

Practice revising a conclusion after a change
Your practice brief was based on the 2025 fixed-date provision. You now have the 2026 amendment and the dated DHS explanation. What should you revise?
A. Keep the original timing conclusion because the purpose of informed choice has not changed.
B. Remove every remaining concern because the new transition language guarantees successful implementation.
C. Revise the timing and implications, retain relevant evidence, and ask what support people and staff still need.
Choose a response to explore the reasoning.

Write a recommendation someone can use
Explain the question and relevant provision. Compare the practical options, including benefits, burdens, and resources.
Recommend an approach and show how community and staff knowledge shaped it.
Name the question that could change your advice.

From a recommendation to a useful change
Ask what staff, partners, and people receiving services need to make the approach work.
Consider preparation, clear responsibilities, usable communication, and follow-through.
Look for evidence of understanding and informed choice, not only a completed activity.

Rewrite the claim with a stronger argument
Claim to revise: “The new requirements ensure that everyone can make informed choices.”
Explain what the record establishes, what people need to use it, and how you would strengthen the recommendation.
Include a meaningful community or staff contribution.

Bring the learning into your responsibility
Analysts: which provision needs closer comparison?
Program and service staff: where could the approach fail in practice?
Fiscal colleagues: whose time or cost is missing?
Managers and leaders: whose knowledge and support are needed?

Make equity visible in the work product
A strong analysis explains the change, examines who is affected, compares reasonable options, and supports a recommendation.
Community knowledge, staff experience, and evidence should influence that reasoning.
Carry one improved question or recommendation into your work.

title: Equity in Budgets, Rates, Contracts, and Procurement
audience: Staff examining resource and purchasing proposals, including legislative analysts, HBCS and other program staff, and the consultant; supervisors and managers examining allocation and implementation.
outcomes: Budgets, rates, contracts, and procurement shape who receives what. Learn to trace where resources and opportunity go, and where uncompensated burden falls, across these financial decisions.
Identify a participation barrier inside a proposed requirement.
Compare allocation or selection options using clear criteria and fitting evidence.
Prepare an equity explanation that preserves actual budget and procurement responsibilities.
summary: Budgets, rates, contracts, and procurement shape who receives what. Learn to trace where resources and opportunity go, and where uncompensated burden falls, across these financial decisions.
body:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Equity in Budgets, Rates, Contracts, and Procurement
Examine what an allocation makes possible, where its burden lands, and what evidence supports a better option.
Advanced self-directed learning

The total does not tell the whole story
Two proposals have the same total budget. One includes usable instructions and staff preparation; the other leaves people to find their own help.

Ask who carries the work outside the total. A smaller agency expense may shift time, difficulty, or cost to someone else.

Four decisions, different equity questions
Budget: what work receives resources?
Rate: how is payment calculated?
Contract: what must be delivered and supported?
Procurement: how can suppliers compete and be assessed?

Examine the purpose, who can participate, and who carries work outside the payment.

Worked example: capacity or the service?
A practice purchasing proposal requires a large administrative office. Its purpose is reliable delivery and reporting.

Compare office size with evidence of delivery, usable records, and reporting capacity. A different route could preserve safeguards without assuming size proves quality.

A requirement larger than its purpose
A practice contract proposal requires a large administrative office to ensure reliable reporting. A smaller organization describes a workable reporting arrangement. What is the strongest equity response?
A. Examine the actual reporting capacity and compare a focused alternative through the applicable process.
B. Keep office size because an established organization is always safer.
C. Remove every reporting safeguard so all organizations can participate.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Follow the burden to its carrier
An instruction may assume spare administrative time, reliable technology, transport, or unpaid help.

Trace whose effort makes the proposal workable. A hidden burden can affect service participation and the staff who repeatedly help people navigate it.

Trace who carries the work
Proposed relationship for practice
1. Proposed requirement
2. Resources paid for
3. Work left outside
4. Who carries that work?
5. Participation to examine
Which assumption about unpaid work needs evidence before comparing options?
A budget total may leave some work outside the agency expense. Examine whether that effort changes practical participation.

A grant and a purchase serve different purposes
A grant supports a public purpose authorized in law. A purchase obtains goods or services for the agency.

Both need clear expectations, but their rules and relationships differ. Identify the arrangement before comparing criteria, payment, reporting, or proposed changes.

A usable invitation is part of participation
A practice opportunity is explained only in an image-based document. An applicant cannot read its requirements with their usual reading tool.

Examine the document and offer a usable explanation through the actual process. Do not infer competence, eligibility, or organizational size from the access difficulty.

Criteria need a reason connected to the work
Identify what each criterion measures and why that matters for the purpose.

Distinguish demonstrated capacity from familiar presentation, existing networks, or polished language. Apply the same relevant questions while examining whether every applicant could understand the invitation.

Worked comparison: the average hides a gap
Practice: four providers each deliver 10 units. Their assumed costs are $80, $120, $100, and $180: $480 total.

Paying $12 per unit gives each $120, also $480 total. The fourth still has a $60 gap. A matched total does not establish adequacy for each provider.

Equal payment, different assumed costs
Practice figures
Invented dollars for 10 units per practice provider
What explains different costs, and what evidence would support a real rate recommendation?
Total assumed costs and payments both equal $480. Equal $120 payments still leave Dune $60 below its assumed cost.

The assumptions behind the figures
Provider
Assumed cost
Payment
Payment minus cost
Aster
$80
$120
+$40
Birch
$120
$120
$0
Cedar
$100
$120
+$20
Dune
$180
$120
−$60
Practice figures
Invented assumptions demonstrate distribution, not actual rate adequacy, eligible cost, quality, or service access. Reasons for differences and later effects are unknown.

When a budget saves by shifting the work
A practice budget removes usable onboarding materials but retains visible development projects. New staff must find their own explanations before joining those projects. What should the analysis examine?
A. Only the agency expense saved; preparation outside the budget is personal responsibility.
B. Preparation burden and access to projects across the employee life cycle, with feasible alternatives.
C. A smaller budget proves that particular employees will not advance.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Workforce resources shape later opportunity
Removing onboarding support and accessible materials may leave new staff doing extra preparation while established staff retain visible assignments.

Trace the connection from recruitment and onboarding to development, performance evidence, advancement, and retention. The proposal’s wording does not establish the later effects.

Compare the saving with the work it shifts
Practice comparison:
A. Remove onboarding materials and keep all project sessions.
B. Keep usable preparation and reduce one session.

Both preserve the available budget. Compare participation, staff effort, necessary preparation, and the value of the session before recommending either.

A fiscal estimate has a defined scope
State budget estimates and wider effects answer related but different questions.

Identify the period, units, assumptions, and costs included. Keep uncounted participant or workforce burden visible as a separate inquiry; do not add it to an official estimate without a fitting basis.

Community knowledge can reveal hidden work
Ask people affected by the proposed allocation what effort the current arrangement requires and what the alternative would change.

Culture briefs can help prepare respectful questions. Actual accounts, not a group description, inform the burden analysis. No partner speaks for every person.

Participation needs a place in the decision
Explain what is open to change, what is already constrained, and how relevant input will be considered.

Receiving comments does not establish influence. Record the substantive concern faithfully and explain how it affects the comparison—or why it cannot yet answer the question.

A community account of the hidden burden
People describe unpaid help needed to complete a practice funding application. A culture brief raised useful preparation questions. Which conclusion best fits the evidence?
A. The brief proves every member of that community needs unpaid assistance.
B. Receiving comments establishes that the revised application will be accessible.
C. The accounts identify a burden to examine; compare usable routes and explain whose experience is present.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Write a resource recommendation people can use
Choose the onboarding budget or reporting-capacity example. Compare two workable approaches to the same purpose.

Explain who benefits, who carries extra work, the safeguard to preserve, and evidence still needed. Name the colleagues whose knowledge would strengthen the recommendation.

Examine use after an actual change
A revised amount or requirement is evidence of a change in the arrangement. Service reach, burden, quality, and participation require their own evidence.

Look for repeated conditions and unintended effects. A favorable total can coexist with an unresolved barrier.

What the payment comparison can establish
Practice figures: four providers receive $120 each. Assumed costs total $480, matching total payments. One provider's assumed cost is $180.

The $60 gap is visible; its cause and an appropriate real rate are not. Explain the distribution before recommending a change.

Reflect on what fairness requires here
Choose a resource decision familiar to you. What purpose does it serve, which conditions make participation possible, and who supplies work outside the budget?

Keep the reflection private if you wish. Identify one necessary safeguard and one assumption worth examining.

A recommendation with substance and limits
Read the total and the distribution. Examine purpose, participation, safeguards, and shifted burden.

Compare workable alternatives and preserve the evidence, assumptions, and actual responsibilities. A supported recommendation makes the next decision clearer without promising an unmeasured result.

title: Responsible Data and Automated Decisions: Evidence before Conclusions
audience: Staff examining research, reports, or automated decision support, including legislative analysts, HBCS and other program staff, and the consultant; supervisors and managers reviewing proposed evidence use.
outcomes: Evidence comes before conclusions. You will learn to define a clear decision question and identify what the available data actually measures before relying on it, including for an automated decision.
Explain missingness, response base, aggregation, and privacy limits.
Examine how an automated rule may repeat an existing process barrier.
Communicate a supported finding with uncertainty and actual responsibility for use.
summary: Evidence comes before conclusions. You will learn to define a clear decision question and identify what the available data actually measures before relying on it, including for an automated decision.
body:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Responsible Data and Automated Decisions: Evidence before Conclusions
Examine what a record measures, whose experience it misses, and whether a proposed decision rule repeats those conditions.
Advanced self-directed learning

What must happen before a record exists?
A person may need to learn about a service, reach an entry route, and have the contact recorded before appearing in a report.

A count can describe the recorded journey while leaving earlier barriers unseen. Ask which experience the proposed decision needs to understand.

Reliability belongs to a purpose
Examine accuracy, completeness, and fit for the intended question.

A record suitable for tracking scheduled appointments may not measure unmet need. Define the decision before judging whether the available information can support it.

Worked example: success becomes a gate
A practice contact-priority tool gives higher priority to people with earlier successful contacts.

Those contacts may partly reflect usable communication and available assistance. Compare the rule with the actual need it is meant to identify; previous visibility is not the same as current need.

When visibility becomes the next gate
Proposed relationship for practice
1. Earlier contact conditions
2. Successful contacts recorded
3. Priority based on history
4. More attention to visible people
5. New contacts reinforce history
Repeated through later records
Where could a usable alternative interrupt the repeated gate?
A historical signal may carry earlier entry conditions into priority and future records. Examine the signal’s fit to current need.

A contact history becomes priority
A practice tool prioritizes people with earlier successful contacts. The test excludes unsuccessful attempts and reports high overall accuracy. What is the strongest recommendation?
A. Examine the omitted attempts, the signal’s fit to need, and errors before relying on this use.
B. Use the score immediately because overall accuracy proves equal access.
C. Treat every person missing from the test as uninterested.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

A blank is not an answer
A missing language field does not mean English is preferred. No response does not mean satisfaction or lack of interest.

Keep missing observations separate and examine how they arise. Repeated defaults can turn incomplete records into misleading decisions.

The denominator defines the finding
Practice: 26 people are invited, 18 respond, and 7 respondents request clarification.

Seven of 18 respondents is 38.9%. The eight missing responses are unknown. This does not estimate the opinion of all invited people or explain nonresponse.

Three counts, three meanings
Practice count
Base
What it describes
What stays unknown
7 concerns
18 respondents
38.9% of respondents
All invitees’ opinions
18 responses
26 invitations
69.2% response coverage
Representation and causes
8 absent answers
26 invitations
30.8% did not respond
Each missing opinion
Practice comparison
Which percentage could you report without changing respondents into all staff?
The base determines the question. Eight missing responses remain unknown rather than becoming satisfied or dissatisfied answers.

A category has a history and a purpose
Trace a field to the question or rule that defined it. What does it record, combine, or leave out?

An operational category does not describe a person’s whole identity, experience, or culture. Reuse needs a fitting question and an actual basis.

Names removed does not mean unrestricted
Combined fields and filters can reveal more than a single table. Removing names does not establish anonymity or authorized sharing.

Clarify the purpose, audience, and applicable protections through the responsible process. A learning exercise supplies no collection or release authority.

Worked comparison: visible work and readiness
A proposed employee dashboard counts visible assignments and rapid responses. Staff have unequal access to those assignments and usable onboarding.

Compare the score with evidence of job-relevant contribution and opportunity to demonstrate it. A high count may describe exposure as well as competence.

A dashboard becomes evidence for advancement
A practice dashboard compares assignment counts and response speed. Staff received different preparation and access to assignments. Which account best supports a readiness discussion?
A. A higher count proves greater competence regardless of access to assignments.
B. Examine job-relevant contribution, opportunity, preparation, and the measure’s limits before interpreting readiness.
C. Collect every employee’s identity information and publish all combinations to find the answer.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Prediction is not a cause or a certainty
A pattern may help estimate a defined result under tested conditions. It does not explain why the result occurs or determine an individual’s future.

Ask what the prediction supports, how uncertainty is conveyed, and whether its use changes the conditions that created the pattern.

Overall accuracy can conceal unequal errors
Examine who is wrongly flagged and who is missed, using an appropriate reference and sufficient evidence.

Compare relevant conditions and groups when the data and permissions support it. A difference invites examination; it does not by itself establish a cause or legal conclusion.

Human review needs an actual opportunity
Someone must be able to question the output, examine relevant evidence, and respond through their actual role.

A signature or an override button does not establish meaningful review. Ask whether the person has information, time, and a usable route to address an error.

Community knowledge tests the meaning
Ask people affected by a measure what the recorded event means in their experience and what the record misses.

Culture briefs help prepare questions about meaning and communication. They do not predict an individual’s answer or certify that a category fits everyone.

Compare responses to the evidence gap
Options include keeping a narrower supported use, examining a better measure, changing a problematic rule, or postponing a consequential use.

Compare purpose, affected people, practical burdens, safeguards, and uncertainty. Do not treat more data or a new model as an automatic remedy.

Community feedback and missing voices
In a sample survey, 7 of 18 respondents request clearer service instructions; 26 people were invited. Community accounts describe an unclear entry route. What conclusion is supported?
A. All 26 invitees agree with the seven respondents.
B. The eight missing answers establish satisfaction, so no further inquiry is useful.
C. The supplied concerns support examining the route; missing opinions and wider prevalence remain unknown.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Prepare an evidence-supported explanation
State the question, source, period, measure, base, missing observations, and proposed use.

Separate description from interpretation and cause. Explain the recurring mechanism, alternatives, permissions that need clarification, and the recommendation’s limits.

Examine the rule after conditions change
A tool’s evidence can become less suitable when entry routes, policies, populations, or recording practices change.

Recheck the proposed use and actual effects through the responsible process. Past testing does not certify every future decision.

Rewrite a finding without losing its value
Original: “38.9% of staff need clearer instructions.”

Supported: “In a practice exercise, 7 of 18 respondents requested clarification; 8 of 26 invitees did not respond.”

What further question would help examine the wording without guessing missing opinions?

Reflect on how a number describes people
Choose a report you know. What is its actual question, and what must happen for someone to enter the count?

Notice an assumption you once made about a number or category. Keep your reflection private, and identify one way to make the explanation more faithful.

Keep meaning with the measure
Use the evidence for a defined question. Retain the base, missing observations, practical conditions, and protections.

Examine whether a repeated rule carries earlier barriers forward. Recommend a fitting response with evidence and uncertainty rather than declaring fairness from a score.

title: Evaluating System Change with a Logic Model
audience: Staff examining program, policy, or workforce change, including legislative analysts, HBCS and other program staff, and the consultant; supervisors and managers considering implementation and results.
outcomes: A logic model makes a change easier to evaluate. Learn to connect the inputs, activities, outputs, outcomes, and intended impact for a clearly defined system change.
Identify an organizational condition that may help or interrupt that connection.
Compare periods or groups without assuming a causal explanation.
Prepare an evaluation account that includes people’s experience, limits, and a justified next inquiry.
summary: A logic model makes a change easier to evaluate. Learn to connect the inputs, activities, outputs, outcomes, and intended impact for a clearly defined system change.
body:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Evaluating System Change with a Logic Model
Connect resources and activities to intended results, examine the conditions between them, and support a justified next inquiry.
Advanced self-directed learning

Begin with a result people can recognize
A service change aims to help people understand their options and receive a usable handoff. A workforce change aims to widen access to meaningful development.

Ask whose experience defines a useful result. A statement of purpose is an intention, not evidence that the result has occurred.

Five connections in the logic model
Inputs: resources. Activities: work performed. Outputs: things produced or contacts completed.

Outcomes: changes in experience or conditions. Intended impact: the broader difference sought. The connections depend on assumptions and context; arrows are not proof of cause.

Worked example: a clearer handoff
Practice inputs: staff preparation and usable materials. Activity: explain a service route. Output: a revised letter and completed explanations.

Intended outcome: people understand the next step and reach a usable handoff. Needed condition: the named route can receive and respond to the contact.

A clearer handoff: intended connections
Proposed relationship for practice
1. Inputs: preparation, materials
2. Activity: explain service route
3. Outputs: guide, explanations
4. Outcome sought: usable handoff
5. Impact sought: equitable access
Which condition must hold between the guide and a usable handoff?
The model makes the intended connections visible. A published guide does not establish understanding or a usable contact route.

A published guide and an unavailable route
A practice service guide clearly names the next contact. People report that the contact route does not respond. What should the evaluation conclude?
A. Publishing the guide proves access improved for everyone.
B. The guide is an output; examine understanding and the usable handoff condition separately.
C. The reports prove that no part of the guide is useful.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Find the assumptions between stages
Ask what must be true for the output to support the outcome. Is a route available, information usable, a responsibility understood, or time provided?

Distinguish a condition supplied by the proposal from one simply assumed. A gap in the connection suggests a question to examine.

The question determines the evidence
“Was the letter revised?” asks about an output. “Could people identify the next step?” asks about understanding. “Did the handoff work?” asks about experience.

Each question needs fitting evidence. Choose a useful question that the available information can answer, and name the questions it leaves open.

Read supplied and missing responses separately
Practice: 30 invitees, 18 responses. Twelve respondents say they can identify the next step; six are unsure. Twelve invitees do not respond.

Twelve of 18 is 66.7% among respondents. Eighteen of 30 is 60% response coverage. Neither supplies the missing opinions or later actions.

Read the response, not a promised result
Practice evidence
Count and base
What it establishes
What it does not
Identifies next step
12 of 18: 66.7%
Supplied respondent answer
Correct real action
Not yet sure
6 of 18: 33.3%
Supplied uncertainty
Reason for uncertainty
Response coverage
18 of 30: 60%
Invitation-set coverage
Representativeness
Absent answers
12 of 30: 40%
No supplied response
Satisfaction or disinterest
Practice comparison
What further question fits the uncertainty without guessing missing opinions?
Supplied uncertainty and missing answers are different. None of these counts establishes a completed service action or the program’s wider impact.

Compare periods without inventing a cause
A before-and-after difference can reflect the change, other conditions, recording practices, or who participated.

Examine comparable definitions, periods, and people. A meaningful descriptive difference can justify inquiry without establishing that one activity caused it.

Worked comparison: development access
In this example, a team opens a development activity to every employee, but some staff lack usable preparation and access to assignments that apply it.

Map invitation → participation → practice opportunity → contribution. An open invitation changes entry wording; the later conditions still need examination.

An open invitation and uneven practice
A practice development invitation is open to all staff. Some employees lack usable preparation and access to practice assignments. Which finding best fits the logic model?
A. The invitation changed entry wording; examine preparation and assignment access before claiming wider opportunity.
B. The open invitation establishes equitable advancement throughout the employee life cycle.
C. People without practice assignments should be rated as less committed.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Use accounts and records for fitting questions
A record may show that a contact happened. A person can explain whether it answered the question or left a barrier.

Keep each account within its scope and examine where evidence agrees or differs. A count does not override meaning, and one account does not represent everyone.

Consider benefits and burden together
A change may improve one route while shifting work or difficulty to another person, team, or stage.

Ask who benefits, who supplies the support, and what unintended effects appear. Examine relevant differences when evidence and protections permit; do not infer them from identity alone.

Protect people while learning from the change
A useful question does not authorize record linkage, new identity questions, or public release.

Clarify actual permissions and responsibilities. Removing names does not establish anonymity, and evaluation does not postpone existing duties or replace assigned decision roles.

Community meaning belongs in the model
Ask people affected by the change what a useful result would mean and which conditions make it possible.

Culture briefs support preparation for respectful questions. Actual accounts inform the model; they do not become fixed group preferences or prove that an intended outcome occurred.

Compare what the findings support doing next
Continue a useful part, revise a weak connection, or investigate an unresolved explanation. Compare each response with the purpose and evidence.

A mixed finding is not automatically failure. Explain the practical alternative, uncertainty, and responsibility that needs clarification.

People define a useful service result
Community participants describe a useful handoff as understanding choices and receiving an answer without repeating their story. A practice report counts completed contacts. What is the best next inquiry?
A. Replace every measure with one participant’s preferred result.
B. Declare the contact total proves that the community’s intended result occurred.
C. Examine whether counted contacts support those experiences, retaining differing and missing perspectives.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.

Connect the model to the intended equity purpose
Use a relevant ADSA goal to explain the purpose of a change and the conditions it seeks to address.

Keep intended results, actual implementation, and observed effects distinct. A goal connection does not certify success, authorize a method, or require every course to address all six goals.

A usable evaluation account
Describe the change, intended result, model, evidence, and conditions. Keep the observation, interpretation, and unresolved explanation separate.

Explain whose experience is present, a practical response, and what would justify revising the conclusion. Preserve actual roles and permissions.

Rewrite an outcome that is only an output
Original: “The new handoff guide improved service access because it was published.”

Supported: “The guide was published. Whether people understood it and reached a usable handoff remains to be examined.”

Which connection and evidence would make the next question useful?

Reflect on a result you would recognize
Choose a change you have experienced at work or in a service. What made the difference meaningful to you?

Keep the reflection private if you wish. Identify one condition between an activity and that result, and one assumption you would want to examine.

Learn whether the connection holds
A logic model explains intended connections. Evaluation examines their conditions and evidence.

Retain useful work, read missing information honestly, and compare practical responses. Intended impact remains an aim until fitting evidence supports an observed change and its explanation.
